articles.body:
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao will appear before the Senate Armed Services Committee on Tuesday as he seeks confirmation to permanently lead the branch.

Cao, a retired Navy captain, took over in April following the ouster of former Navy Secretary John Phelan, who reportedly clashed with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. He is expected to face questions about the war with Iran , military readiness and the USS Abraham Lincoln controversy .

His nomination also requires a congressional waiver because he has not been out of active-duty service for the seven years required by federal law.

The hearing is scheduled to begin at 9:30 a.m. EST.

articles.title: Pentagon fails ninth financial audit in a row
articles.summary: The Pentagon failed its ninth financial audit in a row as many of the department’s financial management systems are outdated and inadequate. The audit included nearly 30 of the department’s components, and it comprised more than $4.8 trillion in assets and involved about 1,500 auditors from the Pentagon’s watchdog and independent public accounting firms, the…
articles.body:
The Pentagon failed its ninth financial audit in a row as many of the department’s financial management systems are outdated and inadequate.

The audit included nearly 30 of the department’s components, and it comprised more than $4.8 trillion in assets and involved about 1,500 auditors from the Pentagon’s watchdog and independent public accounting firms, the department’s watchdog said in a Monday press release .

Several audits are ongoing, and some of the Pentagon’s components have maintained or improved their fiscal 2026 opinions, with the Medicare-Eligible Retiree Health Care Fund receiving the first clean opinion in its history.

“Although the number of material weaknesses appears lower in FY 2026, that reduction stems from consolidation, not resolution,” Brett Mansfield, the Defense Department’s deputy inspector general for audit, said in a statement.

Separately, the Pentagon said on Monday that clean audit opinions will cover more than 56 percent of the department’s assets and more than 90 percent of its liabilities

“The difference from past ventures is that all of the Military Departments and the Office of the Secretary of War are aligned under a single strategy,” Jules W. Hurst III, the Pentagon’s comptroller, said in a statement.

“Rather than relying solely on the Inspector General to conduct the agency-wide audit, the Department has resourced an independent public accountant, as other large federal departments do,” Hurst, who was confirmed in August for the role, said. “Those auditors have specialized data-analysis capabilities that support faster testing, without losing validity.”

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has set a goal for the department to achieve a full, clear audit by 2028.

To help with that, Hegseth has formed an Audit Committee to monitor the Pentagon’s progress toward a clear audit for fiscal 2028, according to the department watchdog.

Outside of the Medicare-Eligible Retiree Health Care Fund getting a first clear opinion, the Pentagon anticipates getting improved opinions in February next year for the following entities: the Navy Working Capital Fund, Defense Information Systems Agency, Defense Intelligence Agency and National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency.

“By centralizing our financial data in the War Data Platform using Advana for Financial Management, we will achieve a higher level of accuracy,” Hurst said.

articles.title: Duffy on calls for new software: ‘This stuff is just really old’
articles.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy reiterated his call for Congress to approve funding for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to upgrade airports and the air traffic control network, stressing that “this stuff is just really old.” Duffy has pressed lawmakers to grant $50 billion in additional funding to go toward making these refurbishments after last week’s…
articles.body:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy reiterated his call for Congress to approve funding for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to upgrade airports and the air traffic control network, stressing that “this stuff is just really old.”

Duffy has pressed lawmakers to grant $50 billion in additional funding to go toward making these refurbishments after last week’s nationwide ground stop of more than 10,000 flights. The disruption followed an attempt to upgrade a copper-wire router with fiber optics in Arkansas.

Another system outage delayed flights through United Airlines on Monday, though the issue was resolved.

“The last [air traffic control] center was built in America –– the newest one I have was built in 1969,” Duffy told Fox News ‘s Sean Hannity, referring to the Anchorage Air Route Traffic Control Center in Alaska. “This stuff is just really old.”

The Transportation secretary said the antiquated software used to manage the U.S. airspace was built in the 1990s, noting that it “works well.”

“But if we’re going to drive more safety and more efficiency, we need a brand-new software,” he continued. “So many developments have been made in the last 30 years.”

Duffy also urged Congress, in a “bipartisan effort,” to “make investments that haven’t been made in decades.”

“So if we get the money, I promise the Congress, America, Donald Trump and I will continue to deliver on these historic investments that change the future of aviation in America, Sean,” he said.

The passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in July 2025 already allocated $12.5 billion to replace aging radar systems, telecommunications and traffic control centers, along with modernizing air traffic control towers and boosting recruitment of controllers.

Congressional Democrats clapped back at the Trump administration by claiming it hasn’t fully justified or explained the need for the additional $50 billion.

“Our air traffic controllers have been failed by Secretary Duffy,” Rep. Rosa DeLauro (Conn.), the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, wrote Sunday on social media . “Friday, thousands of flights were halted with no explanation. Instead of facts, he demanded a $50B ransom with no plan, after $14B in FAA funds sat largely unspent.”

Though Democrats push back on the idea of “build it quickly,” as characterized by Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), the ranking member on the Senate Commerce Subcommittee on Aviation, industry stakeholders have also backed reforms through other legislation, including the Modern Skies Act.

The bill, introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) and Rep. Tracey Mann (R-Kan.) earlier this fall, requests $10.1 billion for air traffic control modernization and $10 billion in improvements to terminals and air traffic control towers, part of a total $30 billion in proposed funding.

articles.title: Lawyer for Fed governor Lisa Cook says she will not participate in 'unfair' White House hearing
articles.summary: In a letter sent to administration officials, Cook's legal counsel Abbe Lowell said Cook has "no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing."
articles.body:
Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook's lawyer informed the White House Monday night that Cook will not participate in a hearing surrounding her possible removal, arguing that the proceeding is unfair and threatens the central bank's independence.

In a letter sent to administration officials, Cook's legal counsel Abbe Lowell said Cook has "no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution's unique status and independence."

The letter comes after President Trump established a committee in August to investigate allegations that Cook committed mortgage fraud and to determine whether her statements constituted legal cause for removal from the Fed.

The White House claims she made false statements or misrepresentations on mortgage applications in 2021 by listing two separate properties as primary residences to secure better loan terms. Cook's legal team contends that her alleged conduct occurred before she took office and therefore does not legally constitute "cause" for her removal from the Fed.

A hearing was originally set for Nov. 5, but it has now come to light that, through almost 20 letters of correspondence over the past few months, Cook's lawyers repeatedly raised concerns and made requests regarding the process that they say the White House has refused to address. A review of the letters exchanged between Cook's attorney and the White House shows the administration did accommodate a change in date, but not other requests made by Cook and her attorney.

"It is unfortunate that your latest correspondence fails to address the concerns Governor Cook has previously raised — making clear that you are uninterested in convening the 'substantive and fair hearing' you have claimed," Lowell wrote. "Instead, you seek only to manufacture 'cause' for a predetermined removal outcome."

Cook's legal team contends that Trump has already decided to fire her, pointing to public statements he made in 2025 and again immediately following a June 2026 Supreme Court ruling that kept Cook in her position but did not foreclose Trump's effort to oust her. The letter also cites remarks from Oct. 10, when Trump was asked why he established the committee reviewing Cook's status.

According to the letter, Trump said Cook is "an automatic no vote" on lowering interest rates, "and that's not a good thing."

articles.title: US agencies confirm investigation into Nvidia partner Megaspeed
articles.summary: The Department of Commerce and Department of Justice (DOJ) confirmed Monday they are investigating Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company at the center of the Nvidia scandal. The Commerce Department began investigating the firm for potential export control violations in 2024 after noticing “suspicious activity” while monitoring for the potential diversion of chips, the agencies…
articles.body:
The Department of Commerce and Department of Justice (DOJ) confirmed Monday they are investigating Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company at the center of the Nvidia scandal .

The Commerce Department began investigating the firm for potential export control violations in 2024 after noticing “suspicious activity” while monitoring for the potential diversion of chips, the agencies said in a joint statement.

After requesting records from Nvidia about its sales to Megaspeed in 2025, the chipmaker placed the company on its “no-sell” list. The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) conducted an “on-site, in-person, end-use check” of the firm in June 2025 and interviewed then-CEO Alice Huang.

Former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with the Megaspeed executive last week following reports that U.S. officials concluded she was working as a Chinese intelligence asset. He resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday amid reports of additional affairs.

The scandal has drawn scrutiny on Megaspeed and concerns about whether it helped smuggle Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls.

After BIS’s June 2025 inspection, the DOJ “took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed,” the agencies noted Monday.

“The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” they wrote.

Megaspeed CEO Tan Yong Pong, who also goes by James Tan, said in a statement last week that the company takes compliance with U.S. export controls “extremely seriously” and is “committed to working constructively and transparently with the U.S. government.”

The firm has retained an American law firm to conduct a “comprehensive census” of its chips and verify compliance, Tan noted.

“Megaspeed welcomes appropriate government scrutiny and is committed to demonstrating through concrete actions that it operates responsibly, transparently, and in accordance with applicable U.S. laws,” he added.

The company has also said Alice Huang left last year, according to The Associated Press.

articles.title: From amusement to apocalypse: The 9 levels of our dangerous digital inferno
articles.summary: With the midterm elections behind us, perhaps we can pivot from the all-too-often tawdry issues that tend to dominate political campaigns and finally deal with the greatest challenge of the century.
articles.body:
With the midterm elections behind us, perhaps we can pivot from the often tawdry issues that to dominate political campaigns and finally deal with the greatest challenge of the century.

Artificial Intelligence IPO disclosures , massive crypto hacks and renegade AI jailbreaks suggest that we are aboard a chaotic ride operated by a handful of entrepreneurs who have no idea how or where the journey ends.

Experts create societal whiplash as they tack between predictions of perpetual exuberance and catastrophic doom. Every person and business is quietly wondering whether they are seeing glimpses of an enlightened future or the worst disaster movie ever made.

Since an embryonic internet was handed off to four universities in 1969 , like the sinners in Dante’s “Inferno ,” we have been toggling through nine levels of technology, each more daunting than the last. While the internet has nurtured technological advancements that have enhanced the quality of life beyond imagination, it has also become a polluted ecosystem where unsavory characters and hostile nations can acquire superpowers and wreak havoc that they could not have in the real world. We are in uncharted territory.

The first of these nine tech levels is the hook — amusement . It seduces users with the euphoria of a Christmas morning as they unwrap sleekly packaged devices, download life-altering software, and wander through the best and worst parts of cyberspace. But this is just the digital appetizer. At the next level, auction, we are invited to purchase almost anything from anyone — whether legitimate or not — with unimaginable efficiency. The accumulation level saw data and dollars increasingly and seamlessly move into cyberspace despite the increased security threats created by relying on an internet never built to be highly secure.

An alignment tier naturally followed, connecting everything in an infinite digital loop. Mobile phones intimately link us to each other, our data and our money, as toasters, refrigerators, cars and pacemakers are networked and harvested for data. The automation level unleashed bots, apps, cookies, clouds and personal assistants, making users more efficient but also more susceptible to viruses, malware, spyware and breaches of their most sensitive data.

The sixth level –— addiction — saw the launch of social media platforms where users, particularly children, were lured and peer-pressured into connecting to one another to enjoy perpetual kumbaya moments and self-validation through “likes” and “dislikes.” Not surprisingly, the digital distance and anonymity available on these platforms also unleashed a primal behavior that decivilizes civilizations. Still, no one said “stop, we need a plan.”

The Aggregation stage brought us a turbocharged offensive on data, solidifying the age of surveillance capitalism . Data is collected, scraped and stolen from browsers, mobile phones, GPS devices, apps, video games and social media platforms and instantaneously sliced, diced, dissected and marketed for profit, political power and criminal mischief. Users naively click “I agree” thinking that they are the beneficiaries when in actually they are digital frogs pinned to a laboratory tray.

The AI level has introduced us to the most formidable and powerful technological developments humans have experienced. Everything that will make us happier, healthier, safer and richer will be driven by AI, as will everything that will hurt, defraud, fool, subjugate and threaten our very existence. AI will usher in the ninth level — the Apocalypse — as the internet and perhaps humanity itself transition to an agentic web where autonomous software agents manage even the most sensitive aspects of our lives.

One of three future scenarios is likely. Mark Zuckerberg argues that humans will continue to control the development and deployment of AI for the betterment of all. Bill Gates and others warn that AI could dominate humans and nudge them toward extinction. Finally, human and nonbiological intelligence may ultimately merge, leading to the next level of human evolutionary existence. That is the future predicted by Ray Kurzweil .

What is most frightening in all of this is the arbitrariness of our predicament. There is no plan to deal with the most consequential moment in human history. We are speeding toward unprecedented decision points without fully knowing whether or how Silicon Valley or Washington is making the decisions and what their true motivations and incentives are. We had ample notice to see all this coming, but we dithered.

Policymakers must recognize priorities and act to ensure that our future is not the result of happenstance. A conclave of public-policy-minded executives and enlightened statesmen representing the democratic nations of the world must agree on a plan, and governments must execute it. We did something similar after World War II when the future of global finance was laid out at Bretton Woods. It worked then and can work again. Our futures and perhaps our lives depend on a plan that does not yet exist.

Now that elections are over, perhaps we can get down to business.

Thomas P. Vartanian is executive director of the Financial Technology and Cybersecurity Center and is the author of “The Unhackable Internet” and “200 Years of American Financial Panics.”

articles.title: Mullin blames tech outages on ‘SI’
articles.summary: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said super intelligence, or “SI”, could be behind the recent technology outages, citing his conversation with an unnamed person from the technology industry. “I started talking to the tech industry,” Mullin said in a Fox News interview, noting that he spoke with a person from the industry who believes “that…
articles.body:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said super intelligence, or “SI”, could be behind the recent technology outages, citing his conversation with an unnamed person from the technology industry.

“I started talking to the tech industry,” Mullin said in a Fox News interview , noting that he spoke with a person from the industry who believes “that it’s the SI, he said, because these programs aren’t designed to work as fast as SI is.”

“When they put in a program that’s able to write codes and it goes in, it self-fixes itself,” he continued. “It’s like doing a change order on a house. When you change one thing in a house, everything else starts changing, that’s a ripple effect. And it causes a system to be overran that weren’t designed to run as fast as the SI technology is today.”

Mullin’s remarks come as Americans recover from widespread technology issues across industries in the past few days impacting flights, banking systems, email and more.

On Thursday, Microsoft users faced global outages that impacted platforms such as Outlook and Teams. The incident, which lasted for about a day, was “introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” the company said.

The Federal Aviation Administration on Friday issued a rare nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours. Authorities attributed the incident to an overload of data on routers, with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy saying a telecommunications line switch by a contractor prompted it.

Customers of several banks including Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo also faced trouble accessing their accounts on Monday.

A spokesperson from JPMorgan Chase told The Hill the cause was “a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems” and denied anything “cyber-related.”

Mullin, during his Fox interview, noted he could say with “98 percent certainty” that the outages were not linked to cyberattack.

“No one’s out there taking claims for it, we’re not seeing the traffic, we’re not seeing the footprints going in, we’re not seeing the footprints going out,” he said.

President Trump, on Tuesday, weighed in on the outages, saying “it’s fine.”

“It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and have all the money, things like that happen,” the president said.

articles.title: Stewart questions Trump administration’s explanation for FAA outage: ‘None of this makes any sense’
articles.summary: Jon Stewart is expressing skepticism about the Trump administration’s explanation for what led to the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) nationwide ground stop last week. The ground stop lasted for several hours on Friday, leading to thousands of flight delays and cancellations. FAA officials later indicated that a router at an Arkansas radio facility was one…
articles.body:
Jon Stewart is expressing skepticism about the Trump administration’s explanation for what led to the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) nationwide ground stop last week.

The ground stop lasted for several hours on Friday, leading to thousands of flight delays and cancellations.

FAA officials later indicated that a router at an Arkansas radio facility was one of two likely reasons for the outage .

In his “The Daily Show” monologue on Monday , Stewart skewered both the response and reason behind the nationwide airline disruption. The Comedy Central host spotlighted remarks Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy made Saturday, when he said, “That router that was being replaced as we switched from copper to fiber, it started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system.”

“I’m guessing that you don’t want us to think about that answer too hard, right?” Stewart said after rolling his eyes.

“About how switching one router in a remote location ends the miracle of human flight as we know it in our country,” the 63-year-old comedian said.

“Hey, you know what fail-safe program we should design our aviation system to mirror? Christmas lights!” Stewart quipped.

“Sorry kids, there’s no Christmas this year: One bulb went dead,” he said to laughter from the audience.

“No fail-safes in the system? No redundancies? Don’t you have a surge protector?” Stewart continued.

“I can’t even order a Crunchwrap Supreme without two-factor authentication. But somehow for the planes, there’s a ‘turn off America’ switch in Arkansas,” Stewart exclaimed.

“This is routine maintenance s—. They’ve replaced 70 percent of the aviation system’s copper wire already, no problems, but now one router,” he said.

“None of this makes any sense,” Stewart said.

articles.title: US 10-Year Yield Set for Historic Run Above 5% on Fed Rate Cycle
articles.summary: The US’s 10-year Treasury yield is nearing its longest run above 5% in almost two decades as investors position for the Federal Reserve to hike interest rate...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The US's 10-year Treasury yield is nearing its longest run above 5% in almost two decades as investors position for the Federal Reserve to hike interest rates more amid stubbornly elevated inflation.

The benchmark for borrowing costs in the world's largest economy is on pace to hold above 5% for the 27th day this year, putting 2026 within striking distance of the 29 such closes recorded in 2007. It was about one basis point higher at 5.14% after US retail sales growth moderated in October.

Upward pressure on yields comes after hotter-than-expected October inflation forced Fed policymakers to begin considering a more aggressively tightening of monetary policy than previously expected.

Traders are now fully pricing a quarter-point rate increase at the central bank's Dec. 9 meeting and see more than 80 basis points of tightening by September 2027, compared with roughly 50 basis points before last week.

Yields back over 5% reflect "risk premium due to uncertainty about the Fed," said Priya Misra, portfolio manager at JPMorgan Asset Management.

The resilient economy and lots of bond sales, from the US government as well as companies looking to invest in AI are other reasons for yields staying above 5%, she said.

The 10-year is a benchmark for the US economy as it helps set the cost of home mortgages, credit cards and business loans. Back in 2007, the 10-year yield climbed above 5% in June and peaked at 5.32% as the Fed kept rates at 5.25% they first reached in July 2006.

That set the stage for elevated rates to weigh on the housing sector, which prompted the central bank to cut rates in September.

For Ian Lyngen, head of US rate strategy at BMO Capital Markets, the current elevated yields are already a cause for concern.

"The impact on the real estate market has been to effectively freeze activity," he said. That's "a foreseeable outcome given the fact that 30-year mortgages have remained above 7% since mid-September."

The trajectory of Treasury yields this year, while not in a straight line, has generally followed an upward path, with the 10-year's rising from under 4% when President Donald Trump launched his war on Iran in late February, disrupting the supply of Middle Eastern oil and gas.

articles.title: Nvidia says it’s policing itself on security, exports
articles.summary: Nvidia’s board of directors announced Tuesday it established an oversight committee focused on national security and export controls following accusations that the company’s former CEO, Jensen Huang, had an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be responsible for “board-level oversight of the company’s national security…
articles.body:
Nvidia’s board of directors announced Tuesday it established an oversight committee focused on national security and export controls following accusations that the company’s former CEO, Jensen Huang, had an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be responsible for “board-level oversight of the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management,” the company said in a blog post .

Suzanne Nora Johnson, who currently serves on Nvidia’s board, was appointed chair of the new committee, which is expected to meet at least quarterly, the tech giant said.

The committee is expected to work with independent third-party experts on law, global trade compliance and national security, it added. The company’s national security and global trade compliance teams will report directly to the standing committee and interim CEO Colette Kress.

The announcement comes as the company faces mounting scrutiny over its chip export policies and global work after reports emerged this month alleging Huang had an extramarital affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials suspect is a Chinese spy.

The woman, Alice Huang, is a former executive of the Singaporean data center and cloud computing firm Megaspeed, which is under investigation over allegations it smuggled Nvidia’s AI chips into China despite export control bans.

Amid the flurry of reports about the alleged affair, Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO of Nvidia last Thursday.

The New York Times reported President Trump was briefed on the U.S. intelligence community’s suspicions about the onetime Megaspeed executive a year ago and chose not to do anything with the information. It is not clear when or what Trump or other administration officials knew about Alice Huang’s potential connection to Jensen Huang.

articles.title: Google: ‘The era of autonomous attacks has arrived’
articles.summary: Google on Tuesday warned the threat posed by autonomous AI models reached a new threshold, ominously stating that “the era of autonomous attacks has arrived.” “Imagine a hacker that doesn’t eat, sleep, or get tired, and never stops searching for a way in,” the company’s Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a statement. “According…
articles.body:
Google on Tuesday warned the threat posed by autonomous AI models reached a new threshold, ominously stating that “the era of autonomous attacks has arrived.”

“Imagine a hacker that doesn’t eat, sleep, or get tired, and never stops searching for a way in,” the company’s Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a statement . “According to the latest AI Threat Tracker report, bad actors are now using autonomous LLM frameworks to continuously scan software updates, figure out what flaw was patched, and build an attack for it — all without human involvement.”

The company’s analysts said the threat level has reached Stage 5, when “multiple attack lifecycle stages” carried out by AI models with at least one human operator involved have occurred.

The GTIG flagged several trends based on incidents involving AI models in recent months, including cyber espionage and impacts on supply chain systems.

Google’s response to these rising risks has been Google AI Threat Defense , “which combines Gemini and other frontier models, Wiz’s context and prioritization, CodeMender’s automated patching, and Mandiant’s expertise to continuously find and fix flaws before attackers can exploit them.”

The GTIG also said its “multifaceted defense strategy integrates” safeguards and containment protocols to keep customers safe and computing infrastructure intact.

John Hultquist, the GTIG’s chief analyst, said in Google’s statement that these attacks do not rely on “groundbreaking methods” to hack through systems, instead taking advantage of “unfixed issues … with much greater speed and scale.”

“Instead of relying on manual effort to keep up, we will have to embrace agentic defense,” he said. “Or we risk falling behind.”

Experts and leaders in the tech industry, along with bipartisan members of Congress, have sounded the alarm about the risks posed by autonomous AI models.

Various attempted and successful hacks in recent months, including the successful breach of technology startup Hugging Face in July, have brought on calls for increased guardrails and legislation to regulate the advanced technology. The Hugging Face incident was the first instance of rogue OpenAI models escaping human prompts and covering its tracks.

The incident prompted California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) to sue OpenAI . He accused the company of disregarding public safety, failing to be transparent with the public and violating California’s Unfair Competition Law. OpenAI pushed back, pointing to its technical report documenting the incident and the rogue agents’ activity.

Any greater cooperation between nations to limit the advancement of AI will be “ more difficult ” than denuclearization talks between the U.S. and the Soviet Union, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates told NBC News in September. He urged Congress to pass legislation regulating AI and said self-moderation from the tech companies is not enough.

articles.title: Iran targets US sites in Bahrain after 2-month pause
articles.summary: Iran on Tuesday fired multiple one-way attack drones toward a U.S. radar facility in Bahrain, marking renewed strikes on American targets in the region after a quiet period of about two months. The drones were intercepted “without any damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel, according to U.S. Central Command, which denied claims…
articles.body:
Iran on Tuesday fired multiple one-way attack drones toward a U.S. radar facility in Bahrain , marking renewed strikes on American targets in the region after a quiet period of about two months.

The drones were intercepted “without any damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel, according to U.S. Central Command , which denied claims from Iran’s Revolutionary Guard that its drones hit a U.S. military radar system.

Bahrain separately said that its air defense systems had successfully intercepted the “treacherous Iranian aerial attacks.”

This marks the third such reported attack in recent days on U.S. interests in Bahrain after Washington and Tehran since September have largely held off on larger-scale barrages against each other, seen in the earlier days of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.

Iran also targeted an American early warning radar facility in the Persian Gulf country on Friday, and a radar system at a U.S. helicopter base there on Sunday. Tehran said the attacks were retaliation for reported U.S. strikes on its communications towers and drone surveillance.

“Continued aggression against the country’s airspace, as well as the use of regional military bases and facilities for hostile acts against Iran, will not go unanswered,” the Revolutionary Guard said in a statement.

President Trump has declared the conflict “effectively over” even as he has not ruled out restarting major combat operations. He also dismissed reports of a “ dirty bomb ” threat on Tuesday, saying the administration was keeping an eye on it.

The U.S. has maintained a naval blockade on Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz since summer, an effort that has crippled Iran’s economy but has come at a significant cost to the Pentagon’s coffers. The total cost of the fight as of Oct. 16 is estimated at $47.1 billion.

Adding to that effort, a third aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, arrived in the region this week along with an air wing of F/A-18E/F Super Hornets and EA-18G Growlers electronic warfare aircraft.

In addition, the U.S. military reportedly carried out a series of secret attacks against Iran in the lead-up to America’s midterm elections. Trump has insisted there is no return to fighting even as the war stretches into its ninth month, has sent fuel costs soaring and is largely blamed for costing Republicans both the House and the Senate in the midterms.

Talks between the two sides, mediated by Qatar, were renewed earlier this month but appear to have stalled yet again.

Trump has said that the U.S. does not need a deal with Iran and has directed Vice President Vance to shift away from focusing on peace talks to the administration’s anti-fraud agenda.

articles.title: Top Nvidia lawyer agrees to testify before Congress
articles.summary: Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, has agreed to appear before Congress next month to discuss chip export controls amid the fallout from ex-CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Three top House Republicans sent a letter Thursday requesting that Teter appear for a “closed-door transcribed interview.” They asked for a response by Friday…
articles.body:
Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, has agreed to appear before Congress next month to discuss chip export controls amid the fallout from ex-CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Three top House Republicans sent a letter Thursday requesting that Teter appear for a “closed-door transcribed interview.” They asked for a response by Friday night, warning that failure to cooperate would result in a subpoena.

“We look forward to meeting with the Chairmen on December 2,” an Nvidia spokesperson said in a statement.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast (R-Fla.), House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party Chair John Moolenaar (R-Mich.) and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) said they want to hear from Teter on AI chip smuggling and “adversary military use” of the company’s products.

The trio also indicated they want to discuss recent reports of “interference in U.S. export control policies and investigations, including those involving Megaspeed.”

A source familiar with discussions said Nvidia previously offered for Teter to appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee in July, October and earlier in November on AI chip diversion, export controls and Megaspeed, but the panel declined.

Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company, is currently under investigation by the Department of Commerce and the Department of Justice (DOJ) over its compliance with export controls amid concerns about the potential diversion of chips to China.

The New York Times reported last week that Teter reached out to agents working on the case last year, saying Under Secretary of Commerce Jeff Kessler had given the company permission to reach out. Shortly after, the case was transferred to the DOJ, according to the Times.

The agencies said Monday that the Justice Department “took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed” following an on-site inspection of the company last June.

The scrutiny on the firm comes after Huang admitted last week to having an affair with a former Megaspeed executive who is suspected of working as a Chinese intelligence asset.

Huang, who stepped down as CEO on Thursday, has also agreed to appear before Congress on Dec. 1.

“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” Crawford, Mast and Moolenaar said in a statement Tuesday.

“The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous PRC [People’s Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal,” they continued.

articles.title: US loses measles elimination status after more than 25 years
articles.summary: The U.S. on Tuesday officially lost its measles elimination status for the first time since it gained this distinction more than 25 years ago, with a count of more than 7,700 cases in the past two years and more than 10 deaths reported by states since 2025. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) made the…
articles.body:
The U.S. on Tuesday officially lost its measles elimination status for the first time since it gained this distinction more than 25 years ago, with a count of more than 7,700 cases in the past two years and more than 10 deaths reported by states since 2025.

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) made the announcement in a media briefing Tuesday, following a three-day meeting the global health organization held with the U.S. and Mexico over their respective measles elimination statuses with PAHO’s Measles and Rubella Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission.

“The commission concluded that the endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn, a recommendation which I have accepted,” Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO’s director, said during the briefing.

PAHO officials acknowledged that with this loss of status, the U.S. is officially considered a country where measles is endemic. While PAHO does not recommend any changes to travel guidance with this loss of status, officials noted it does indicate a country should be dedicating resources toward combatting measles.

The Wall Street Journal reported last week, citing anonymous sources, that PAHO concluded the U.S. had lost its measles elimination status.

For infectious disease and public health experts, Tuesday’s announcement was a foregone conclusion. A country technically loses its elimination status after experiencing 12 months of sustained domestic transmission, which the U.S. recorded in January. And since then, the number of infections has only gone up, more than doubling last year’s count.

Since the start of 2025, states including Texas, New Mexico, New York, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin have reported measles-related deaths. For most states, these have been the first measles-associated deaths they’ve reported in decades.

PAHO had initially scheduled the meeting between the U.S. and Mexico for April, but it rescheduled to November to give the U.S. more time to complete viral genome sequencing.

While public health advocates have called this development a “tragedy,” administration officials have sought to downplay the significance of losing measles elimination status.

Ralph Abraham, a former Louisiana surgeon general who briefly served as the principal deputy director at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) earlier this year, said losing this status was “not really” a significant loss.

CDC Director Erica Schwartz has said that losing elimination status will not change the federal response to the measles outbreaks, which has been criticized for being tepid . Health leaders have repeatedly called for a robust measles vaccination campaign at the national level to combat the measles outbreaks across the country, while Trump administration officials have questioned the safety and efficacy of the vaccine or equivocated vaccine injuries with measles deaths.

Following the Tuesday announcement, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. wrote on social media , “We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.”

He noted that childhood immunizations were disrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic, pointing to other countries that have also lost their measles elimination statuses like Armenia, Austria and Uzbekistan.

“We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust. We will answer families’ questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment,” he added.

Kennedy’s own response to the measles outbreaks has been marked by online spats with state leaders like Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D), who blamed the secretary and the rest of the Trump administration for worsening the conditions that led to the return of measles. Shapiro claimed that Kennedy went on a “tirade” when the governor urged him to encourage people to get vaccinated.

In her own statement on Tuesday, Schwartz said, “The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does.”

“We know where transmission is occurring and we’ve invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities,” she added. “Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.”

Any country that loses its elimination status must submit a corrective action plan to PAHO, outlining their proposed strategy for regaining elimination.

“Of course, we are expecting many, many in many countries to increase the capacities of surveillance so that the system can be sensitive enough to detect in a timely basis any new cases,” said Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO’s Comprehensive Immunization Special Program.

“But not just that, we need to have a rapid response for each case that is detected, and of course we need more social participation, more national coordination, interstate coordination, to have vaccines on a timely manner as well,” he added.

Salas said he expects the countries will present their corrective action plans to PAHO in the coming weeks.

One year after losing its elimination status, Canada’s measles outbreak was declared over in October, but this does not signify the immediate return of its status as a country where the disease is eliminated.

“The end of this multi-jurisdictional outbreak does not automatically restore Canada’s measles elimination status. Canada can regain this status once transmission of the measles strain associated with the outbreak has been interrupted for at least 12 consecutive months,” a spokesperson for the Public Health Agency of Canada said in a statement to The Hill.

Democratic lawmakers sharply criticized the Trump administration over the status loss.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), who is expected to be the upper chamber’s next majority leader when Democrats regain control of Congress in January, said during floor remarks Monday that it took Kennedy and President Trump “less than two years to undo decades of work into eliminating measles in America.”

“The resurgence of this dangerous virus is a direct consequence of the pathological stupidity plaguing this administration,” Schumer added.

Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D-S.C.), a pediatrician, said Sunday that “no child should have to suffer from a disease we know how to prevent because of political hubris in Washington.”

articles.title: Banning phones really does help kids learn, researchers say
articles.summary: A new nationwide analysis of school cellphone bans found they can add the equivalent of one to two weeks of learning for students.
articles.body: A new nationwide study found that in-school cellphone bans can lead to modest improvements in learning. Now, researchers want to understand whether kids’ phone use outside the classroom might contribute to the rest of students’ learning loss — using the conditions of Meta’s multibillion-dollar settlement from earlier this year. Banning cellphones in schools has the equivalent effect of adding one to two weeks of school to the academic year, accounting for about half of the learning loss students experienced in the US between 2013 and the 2020 covid-19 pandemic, according to the study carried out by researchers from Harvard University and Dartmouth College in partnership with academic assessment group NWEA. The group analyzed testing data from 3.3 million students across 4,600 schools between the 2021–22 school year and 2025–26, including schools with and without phone bans. Though modest, such a finding is exactly the kind of effect researchers were seeking, says Tom Kane, faculty director of the Harvard University Center for Education Policy Research. While previous studies about cellphone bans in school found positive effects on academic outcomes, many of them examined schools outside the US. An earlier nationwide US study looked at academic outcomes based on averages within schools, whereas this latest study looked at student-level data, which the researchers said allowed them to control for more factors and observe the effect of the bans on students who were experiencing the most or least learning loss. In addition to potentially answering questions about the impact of a major new technology on learning, the findings show that cellphone bans can be a cost-effective way to improve student outcomes. While purchasing lockable pouches for a class of 17 students would cost an estimated $425 per teacher, the researchers found, paying an average teacher’s salary for an extra week would be $2,080. Many parents and teachers already have a hunch — popularized by academics like social psychologist Jonathan Haidt — that cellphones and social media have impacted their kids’ learning and mental health. But Kane says it’s still important that scientists get the chance to actually test that hypothesis. Prior to his in-school cellphone ban study, Kane believed that a de-emphasis on test-based accountability in US schools was largely to blame for learning loss. But as he looked into it further, he changed his mind after seeing that kids outside the US were also experiencing learning loss. Through this recent study, Kane found much of it is attributable to in-school cellphone use. Kane was surprised by some of the findings in this latest study. For example, the in-school bans had similar effects on learning gains for students across different age groups, who have different amounts of experience with phones, and researchers did not find a big difference in the impact of the phone bans between students across achievement levels. Differences between lower- and higher-achieving students might instead be explained by out-of-school cellphone use, Kane says, and that out-of-school phone use could account for some of the remaining learning loss across the board. Testing that hypothesis would be far more difficult because there’s no equivalent ban on out-of-school phone use. But Kane believes there’s a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to try. This summer, as part of a $17.1 billion settlement with nearly every US state, Meta agreed to implement sweeping restrictions on users under 18. Many of the restrictions are expected to take effect within the next few months, and among other changes, they limit the amount of time teens can spend on Meta’s apps by default. Kane believes that could provide researchers a before-and-after look into the impact of out-of-school social media use, in the same way the phone bans let them study the impact in schools. If researchers are able to check that teens really were using social media less outside of school (rather than their parents turning off the default limits, for example) and link that to academic outcomes at different schools, it could provide a better understanding of how much out-of-school cellphone and social media use accounts for the rest of kids’ learning loss, Kane says. “Now that we’ve learned something about the effect of in-school phone use, it makes it even more frustrating how little we know about the actual impact of out-of-school phone use,” Kane tells The Verge in an interview. “We are 13 years into a substantial loss in achievement in the US, and a prime suspect that a lot of parents would probably point to is this out-of-school cellphone use.” There are two significant limitations. The settlement doesn’t offer an easy way to tell whether teens are in fact using Meta’s platforms less or — if they are — whether they’ve simply transferred that screen time to other apps. To understand the effect on students’ academic outcomes, researchers would also need to be able to link the restrictions with changes in kids’ achievement at school. The settlement includes an incentive for attorneys general to strike similar deals with TikTok and YouTube, which so far have declined to implement such restrictions, but if they did, that could help address the first problem. And platforms, Kane says, could help with the second problem by sharing de-identified and aggregated data with researchers, organized by school or another kind of subgroup. It’s a big ask, but Kane says this may be the best chance to study important questions about the impact of social media. “I spent the whole summer trying to identify other sources of data for this, and I just struck out,” Kane says. “This Meta settlement is the clearest path forward for trying to answer that important question.” And if research shows that out-of-school cellphone use is not fully or even mostly to blame for the rest of the drop in academic performance, the findings would prod researchers to look for other theories. “I’m sure that there are surprises, questions we haven’t even realized,” Kane says. “That’s one reason to want to know because people have these hunches, but I’m sure some of these hunches are wrong. But a second reason is we actually don’t know that the restrictions currently in the Meta settlement are going to be effective.” While AGs attempted to craft what they believed would be the most effective guardrails for the settlement, Kane says, we don’t yet have the data to prove whether those guesses will bear out. “I think a lot of people are hoping that restrictions on cellphone use after school would produce increases in student engagement, but we won’t actually know that unless we collect these data,” Kane says. “This settlement is set to expire in 10 years. Let’s use this time to build an evidence base on the effect of restrictions.”

articles.title: The DOJ says it’s investigating Megaspeed
articles.summary: The Justice and Commerce departments released an update on their investigation of Megaspeed, following Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO.
articles.body: The Justice and Commerce Departments said that they are investigating Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data center company intertwined with the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, after reporting suggested an investigation had been halted last year. “While we don’t typically comment on ongoing investigations, it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting,” the departments said in a statement issued Monday evening. The departments acknowledged there’s been “significant public attention” on Megaspeed. Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO last week after reports he had an affair with former Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, who Megaspeed says left the company in August 2025. The scandal has raised questions about national security, and sparked scrutiny of Nvidia’s handling of exports of its chips to China and Megaspeed’s possible role in moving along Nvidia’s chips. Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that a Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed “came to a sudden halt” late last year after its investigators received an email from Nvidia’s general counsel, claiming Commerce Department official Jeffrey Kessler gave Nvidia permission to reach out. The case was then “quickly” handed over to the DOJ, according to the Times. The announcement today says the DOJ took the “lead role” in the investigation last year: > After identifying suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential sensitive semiconductor diversion, the Department of Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations. In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list. Based on the Department of Commerce’s investigation, agents from the Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, conducted an on-site, in-person, end-use check at Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed CEO Alice Huang. Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed. The statement doesn’t go into detail about the current status of the case, but it says the DOJ and Commerce Department “will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred.”

articles.title: Jensen Huang breaks silence on resignation, says he’d be ‘honored’ to return as Nvidia’s CEO
articles.summary: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang broke his silence on Tuesday following his resignation from the company, stating he would be “honored” to return to the role should the company’s Board of Directors support the move. In a statement obtained by The Hill, Huang said he saw an “outpouring of calls” from some Nvidia staff, investors,…
articles.body:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang broke his silence on Tuesday following his resignation from the company, stating he would be “honored” to return to the role should the company’s Board of Directors support the move.

In a statement obtained by The Hill, Huang said he saw an “outpouring of calls” from some Nvidia staff, investors, business partners and customers for him to return as CEO, just days after he resigned from the role amid a national security scandal.

“Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company,” Huang wrote. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

A source familiar told The Hill on Monday Nvidia’s Board of Directors is not weighing Huang’s return.

Huang resigned days after admitting to an extramarital affair, and reports suggest it was with executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials suspected was a spy for China. The allegations sparked a flood of scrutiny of the longtime CEO, including an independent investigation by Nvidia’s Board of Directors.

Alice Huang is a former executive of the Singaporean data center and cloud computing firm Megaspeed, which is under investigation over allegations it smuggled Nvidia’s AI chips into China despite chip export controls.

Jensen Huang said on Tuesday he “did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life.”

“I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation,” he wrote.

Shortly after his resignation, petitions circulated calling for his return, while President Trump said on Monday he “certainly wouldn’t mind” if Huang returned as CEO.

“I think he learned a big lesson,” Trump said. “I guess maybe one lesson more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that.”

The Financial Times reported over the weekend he is discussed a comeback with allies in Silicon Valley. Several tech executives signed an open letter calling for his reinstatement, including SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan.

The executives argued Huang should be brought back while an independent investigation is completed.

The open letter, which has more than 170,000 signatories, asked the board to “provide compelling evidence that [Huang’s] removal is in Nvidia’s best interests,” and stated the former CEO “deserves due process, not mob justice.”

articles.title: Leavitt: White House needs to ‘calm the temperature’ after nationwide tech outages
articles.summary: Former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt called on the White House to be more transparent regarding to the nationwide tech outages in recent days, advising officials to spread their message “wide and loud.” “What I would say to the White House is transparency is key,” Leavitt said during a Fox News appearance. “It’s going…
articles.body:
Former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt called on the White House to be more transparent regarding to the nationwide tech outages in recent days, advising officials to spread their message “wide and loud.”

“What I would say to the White House is transparency is key,” Leavitt said during a Fox News appearance . “It’s going to help the country grapple with what’s going on.”

The former press secretary said “there should be a message directly to the American people” from either President Trump or a White House official explaining “what they know and what they believe to be true to really calm the temperature.”

Americans are still recovering from widespread technology issues across industries in the past few days which have impacted flights, banking systems, email and more.

One of the most consequential incidents was the Federal Aviation Administration issuing a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday that lasted more than four hours. Authorities attributed the incident to an overload of data on routers. Thousands of flights were delayed and cancelled on Friday, impacting flight operations through the weekend.

On Thursday, Microsoft faced global outages that impacted its flagship platforms such as Outlook and Teams. The incident, which lasted about a day, was “introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” the company said.

Customers of several banks including Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo also faced trouble accessing their accounts on Monday. A spokesperson from JPMorgan Chase told The Hill the cause was “a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems” and denied anything “cyber-related.”

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said super intelligence could be the reason behind the tech outages but noted he could say with “98 percent certainty” that the outages were not linked to cyberattack.

Trump, on Tuesday, weighed in on the outages, saying “it’s fine.”

“It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and have all the money, things like that happen,” the president said.

articles.title: Proton's Lumo, a privacy-focused alternative to ChatGPT and Claude, arrives on desktop | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Proton's new Lumo Desktop app for Windows, Mac, and Linux lets users automate tasks across files and connected apps, with granular controls over what its AI can access.
articles.body:
Proton , the privacy-focused tech company offering alternatives to Google’s and Microsoft’s tools for email, productivity apps, password management, cloud storage, and more, is now bringing its AI app Lumo to personal computers. On Tuesday, the company launched Lumo Desktop for Windows, macOS, and Linux, allowing users to leverage its AI to carry out local tasks on their computer involving connected apps, personal files, and other automations.

The app is designed to offer users more control over their personal data, as consumer AI technology becomes focused more on AI agents that can perform tasks on users’ behalf, rather than just answering questions.

Already, the major model makers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and others, offer desktop tools for working with their AI technologies, but doing so invites increased risk to users’ personal data . Only this week, for instance, Apple announced it was addressing those privacy concerns with tightened security settings for apps that request Full Disk Access, as the AI desktop apps do.

Proton’s idea is to offer a set of tools that let its AI access connected apps, files, and folders and automate tasks, but with more personalization over how much access the AI has. The company says users can choose which actions the AI agent takes that will need to request their approval, and it vows that the conversations and information from connected apps and files are never used to serve personalized ads or train AI models.

The new app includes a variety of connectors that support local tools, like file-system access, shell execution, and browser content fetching, as well as Proton’s email app and other third-party services, including Confluence, Dropbox, and Jira.

The connectors also support local and remote MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers, which AI agents use to access external data sources.

Proton says that users can decide for each connector which actions Lumo can perform automatically, which require approval, and which are blocked entirely. Users can also turn individual tools off from the Tools menu in their conversation.

In addition, users can set up their own scheduled tasks, where each has its own set of permissions, in terms of what can be handled automatically and what requires approval.

Proton notes that it uses encryption to ensure that only users can read their chat history, not the company. The company also says it keeps no server-side logs, and the limited data it does store is protected under Swiss privacy law. The data is hosted on European infrastructure, outside the scope of the U.S. CLOUD Act , which specifies how law enforcement agencies access data held by cloud service providers.

The company says it’s investing in its infrastructure, with its first Nvidia B300 cluster built on Open Compute Project (OCP) standards now going live in Switzerland.

Similar to other AI apps, Lumo’s desktop app supports Skills, which lets users save instructions, templates, and reference files that Lumo can reuse across their conversations. (An earlier version of this, Custom Lumos, will now be migrated to the Skills format.)

articles.title: Democrats go after Trump administration over US losing measles elimination status
articles.summary: Democratic lawmakers are going after the Trump administration after a global health organization announced the U.S. has officially lost its measles-free status. On Tuesday, the U.S. lost its measles elimination status for the first time since it earned the designation more than 25 years ago. In the last two years, the U.S. has racked up…
articles.body:
Democratic lawmakers are going after the Trump administration after a global health organization announced the U.S. has officially lost its measles-free status.

On Tuesday, the U.S. lost its measles elimination status for the first time since it earned the designation more than 25 years ago. In the last two years, the U.S. has racked up more than 7,700 cases of measles, and states have reported more than 10 deaths related to the disease since 2025.

The Pan American Health Organization made the announcement about the U.S.’s status during a Tuesday media briefing.

“For 26 years, measles was eliminated in the United States—until [President] Trump and [Health and Human Services Secretary] RFK Jr. [Robert F. Kennedy Jr.] turned back the clock and brought a deadly, preventable disease roaring back. This is outrageous. Measles cases are at record highs, ten people have died from measles this year, including infants,” Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) said in a Monday statement.

“Instead of doing everything in his power to stop this, RFK Jr. has accused state health officials of exaggerating the outbreak, suggested the deaths may have been ‘fabricated,’ and changed how the CDC [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention] counts measles deaths—Americans deserve real leadership, not a coverup,” she added.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), who is expected to be the upper chamber’s next majority leader when Democrats regain control of the Senate in January, said during floor remarks Monday that “it took Trump and RFK [Jr.] less than two years to undo decades of work into eliminating measles in America.”

“Over the weekend, it was announced the United States lost its measles elimination status, a public health achievement that we were so proud of to have secured over two decades ago,” Schumer added. “The resurgence of this dangerous virus is a direct consequence of the pathological stupidity plaguing this administration.”

In his own Monday statement, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) said the loss of the elimination status “is the tragic yet predictable result of an ongoing campaign by grifters, quacks and charlatans to put their own greed and self-worth ahead of the health and safety of children.”

Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D-S.C.), a pediatrician , slammed the loss of the elimination status in a social platform X post Sunday.

“As a pediatrician, I saw firsthand how decisions made in Washington hurt our children and families. Nothing makes that clearer than this,” Andrews wrote on X.

“No child should have to suffer from a disease we know how to prevent because of political hubris in Washington,” she added.

Sen. Michael Bennet (D-Colo.) in a statement called on CDC Director Erica Schwartz to resign, accusing her of offering “excuses and complacency” rather than mounting an urgent response to protect children.

In the House, the Democratic Doctors Caucus said the decision to remove measles elimination status was “directly linked to the doubt and misinformation that HHS [Health and Human Services] Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has spread surrounding vaccines.”

“Under his leadership, deadly, preventable diseases like measles are back,” the group of lawmakers said in a statement. The caucus includes Democratic Reps. Ami Bera (Calif.), an internal medicine specialist; Kim Schrier (Wash.), a pediatrician; and Maxine Dexter (Ore.), a pulmonologist.

The caucus “will do everything we can with our new Democratic majorities in Congress to hold RFK Jr. accountable, rebuild our public health infrastructure, and save lives,” the lawmakers continued.

In a statement, Schwartz pointed to the $100 million infusion the agency sent to states to help them respond to outbreaks of measles and other vaccine-preventable diseases. “The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” the CDC director’s statement said. “Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.”

Kennedy said in a post on X Tuesday afternoon that the HHS “will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status.”

“I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles,” he added.

articles.title: What is a dirty bomb? What to know about reported Iran threat
articles.summary: A dirty bomb combines conventional explosives with radioactive material but cannot produce a nuclear explosion.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — A reported Iranian plan involving a potential “dirty bomb” attack in Washington, D.C., is raising questions about what the weapon is, how it works and the dangers it could pose.

President Trump told reporters Tuesday the U.S. takes the potential threat from Iran “very seriously because they happen to be crazy.” He didn’t say the threat was credible or imminent, but he did threaten Tehran.

CNN reported , citing sources, that U.S. intelligence indicates Iran is developing plans to potentially detonate a dirty bomb in Washington, D.C.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson denied the report Tuesday in a post on social platform X , calling the allegations “baseless.”

So, what exactly is a dirty bomb, and how dangerous could one be?

A dirty bomb is a mix of explosives, such as dynamite, combined with radioactive material, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Unlike a nuclear weapon, a dirty bomb doesn’t produce an atomic explosion. Instead, it uses explosives to scatter radioactive dust, smoke or other material into the surrounding area.

The goal is to spread radioactive contamination rather than trigger a nuclear reaction, the CDC noted.

The immediate danger from a dirty bomb would likely come from the conventional explosion itself, which could cause serious injuries, deaths and property damage to people nearby, according to the CDC.

Radioactive materials used in a dirty bomb generally wouldn’t produce enough radiation exposure to cause immediate serious illness in most people outside the immediate blast area.

However, radioactive dust and smoke could spread beyond the explosion site. Inhaling or coming into contact with contaminated material could pose health risks.

Radiation cannot be seen, smelled, felt or tasted, making it difficult to determine whether an area has been contaminated without specialized equipment.

How often does the US receive dirty bomb threats?

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told CNN the administration is “monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland.”

Rep. André Carson (D-Ind.) who serves on the House Intelligence Committee, also told the outlet Monday that lawmakers receive “these kinds of reports quite often,” but many do not become public.

Another source told CNN that Iran understands an attack on the U.S. could trigger retaliation.

Officials have reportedly discussed possible countermeasures related to the potential threat in Washington, along with contingency planning for threats in the Middle East.

articles.title: Musk: Duffy declined offer of free Starlink for FAA

As it turns out, they were,” Musk wrote in a post on the social…
articles.body:
Space X CEO Elon Musk said on Monday that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy turned down a “Free Starlinks” offer for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

“Free Starlinks for FAA were offered to Sec Duffy, but he said they were not needed. As it turns out, they were,” Musk wrote in a post on the social platform X .

Musk’s comments come after the FAA issued a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday that lasted over four hours. Authorities attributed the incident to an overload of data on routers.

A day after the incident in a press briefing, Duffy said a telecommunications line switch may have started the ground stoppage, noting contractor L3Harris had been replacing an older copper wire with a new fiber cable.

On Sunday, the FAA said preliminary findings point to the router in El Dorado, Ark., and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas to be likely reasons for the excessive data flooding the systems.

“We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel,” L3Harris, the current network provider for the FAA, said in a statement on Saturday. “L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”

Duffy claimed that he cannot cancel the contract with L3Harris, adding, “I want to get away from L3Harris and get to a new one, but they own the network. I can’t cancel the network that they own.”

Last year, the FAA said that it was not considering replacing its current L3Harris and Verizon contracts with Musk’s Starlink, according to a Reuters report .

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the agency “would not use Starlink (or any satellite service) as the sole communications technology for safety-critical air traffic services.”

Starlink was pulled into the center of a controversy last month after Ukraine’s military faced restricted access to Starshield, the military version of the satellite-based system. This impacted the capabilities of Ukraine’s drones, airplanes and helicopters.

Following Friday’s incident, Duffy asked Congress for $50 billion to update the U.S.’s “incredibly old” air traffic control systems. His demands were echoed by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and House Speaker Mike Johnson.

“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Duffy said. “Let’s not do a patchwork, a fix to a system that’s critical for every single family.”

articles.title: ‘The time to get it done is now’: Lawmakers stress urgency on permitting reform bill
articles.summary: Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are banding together to stress the need for Congress to act now and pass a major bipartisan permitting reform bill, before the makeup of the legislative branch changes next year. At The Hill’s Bipartisan Blueprint event Tuesday, members of Congress tied the bill — the Bipartisan American Affordability…
articles.body:
Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are banding together to stress the need for Congress to act now and pass a major bipartisan permitting reform bill , before the makeup of the legislative branch changes next year.

At The Hill’s Bipartisan Blueprint event Tuesday, members of Congress tied the bill — the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) — directly to Americans’ concerns about rising costs coming out of the midterms.

“This last election said a lot when people talk about affordability,” Rep. Harriet Hageman (R-Wyo.) told The Hill’s Rachel Frazin. “You don’t have affordability unless you have reliable and affordable energy.”

The Senate advanced the BAAJA on Monday night in a vote that showed bipartisan support for the legislation. Senators voted to invoke cloture 70-27 on the substitute amendment sponsored by Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), the chair of the Environment and Public Works Committee.

That sets up a final vote for the legislation in the Senate, but it would still need to get through the House and be signed by President Trump.

Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), ranking member of the Energy and Natural Resources Committee and one of the bill’s co-sponsors, said the Senate may still amend the bill’s text before final passage.

In the House, the bill faces opposition from both sides, though lawmakers at the event Tuesday remained optimistic.

“It’s 70-plus votes in the Senate, and I think that that bodes well in the House for both Republicans and Democrats to recognize that this truly is one of those compromise bills that benefits everyone,” Hageman said.

The bill would speed the construction of energy, mining and infrastructure projects, while limiting environmental challenges under the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act.

The legislation faces opposition from some House Democrats, including Reps. Jared Huffman (Calif.), Adelita Grijalva (Ariz.), Summer Lee (Pa.), Melanie Stansbury (N.M.) and Rashida Tlaib (Mich.).

Huffman, who is in line to chair the House Natural Resources Committee, says the bill would constrain National Environmental Policy Act reviews, radically alter transmission approvals and let companies sue the government for damages if they can show they were discriminated against on the basis of fuel type.

Trump’s opposition to wind turbines had also left some of the bill’s proponents worried.

Rep. Vicente Gonzalez (D-Texas) said Congress should take action now because a better bill may never come.

“This is not a bad deal, and the time to get it done is now,” Gonzalez told Frazin. “You may look for a better day down the road, and then that day never gets here. … We’ve been waiting for this way too long, and I think the American people deserve action from Congress.”

The bill’s proponents argue lengthy environmental reviews and litigation can hold up permitting of infrastructure and energy projects for decades.

Heinrich, asked about a wind turbine project in New Mexico that took 17 years to permit and build, said he believed the new legislation would have had it done in five years.

“If you have all the boxes checked, like this is one of the best-designed projects that I’ve had to engage with, and it still took 17 years, you know that something’s wrong,” Heinrich said.

Some Republicans fear the BAAJA could lead to more renewable energy projects, specifically wind, and Democrats worry it may lead to more fossil fuel projects that could harm the environment.

Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) sees it differently, arguing the BAAJA levels the playing field between energy sources and encourages production of all types.

“This is fuel neutral,” Cramer said. “We truly do need whatever fuel we can use at any particular spot to generate electricity at a good cost.”

“I think what it locks in is that there’s a system and a process for determining the best source at any given moment,” he later added.

Hageman said she sees the bill as delivering incentives for both parties.

“If California wants wind power, they’re going to have to find a way to get it there. And if we can’t build the projects in Wyoming, they’re not getting that power,” Hageman said. “That, to me, is the bipartisan support for this.”

Gonzalez represents Corpus Christi, Texas, which has been nearing a water crisis for months and is hoping to build desalination plants that have been stalled for years.

“We want to try to make the process as smooth as possible,” Gonzalez said. “We’ll be able to produce more energy, we’ll be able to create a lot of new jobs. I think it’ll be transformative, and it’s been a long time coming.”
