Apple’s Support System Status page shows issues or outages with the App store, Apple Music, AppleCare and iCloud.

The outage is just the latest in a growing list of technology issues sweeping the globe. Earlier on Tuesday, iPhone users who visited nearly 200 websites were subjected to “malicious” malware in a cryptocurrency scheme.

The malicious code reportedly targeted users on some of the world’s most-visited websites, including those of Zoom, HSBC, Equifax, CNN, Salesforce and Ikea, through the website optimization platform Optimizely.

The company confirmed the incident, saying ​it had identified “a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a ⁠vulnerability in Experimentation and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”

It also follows similar issues with Microsoft last week and recent disruptions to operations at Bank of America, Chase and Wells Fargo.

Apple has not yet responsed to a request for comment.

articles.title: FAA halts router upgrades after ground stop fuels infrastructure concerns
articles.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration has halted router upgrades following a nationwide ground stop last week, which officials say stemmed from an overload of data on routers. The agency paused the Jupiter router installation as it continues to assess the cause behind Friday’s incident, according to NewsNation, the Hill’s partner. The Wall Street Journal reported on…
articles.body:
The Federal Aviation Administration has halted router upgrades following a nationwide ground stop last week, which officials say stemmed from an overload of data on routers.

The agency paused the Jupiter router installation as it continues to assess the cause behind Friday’s incident, according to NewsNation, the Hill’s partner.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday also said the pause will be in place while assessing what went wrong, citing an FAA official.

The rare nationwide ground stop issued Friday lasted over four hours causing thousands of flight cancellations and delays across the nation through the weekend. On Saturday, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a telecommunications line switch may have started the ground stoppage, noting contractor L3Harris had been replacing an older copper wire with a new fiber cable.

On Sunday, the FAA said preliminary findings point to the router in El Dorado, Ark., and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas to be likely reasons for the excessive data flooding the systems.

L3Harris, the current network provider for the FAA, said in a statement on Saturday that the company is “supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel.”

Following the incident, Duffy asked Congress for $50 billion to update the U.S.’s “incredibly old” air traffic control systems. His demands were echoed by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and House Speaker Mike Johnson.

GOP Rep. Tim Burchett (Tenn.) also called on the Republican leadership to pass legislation funding air travel infrastructure updates saying, “The problem you’re going to have, I think, is with the Senate.”

Burchett pointed to the ALERT Act , which was created in response to the fatal 2025 collision between an Army helicopter and a commercial jet near Reagan Washington National Airport. The legislation passed in the House in April but has yet to receive a vote in the upper chamber.

On Tuesday, following a press conference with the families of the victims of the 2025 crash, Duffy told reporters that “a new architecture for telecom is important,” adding, “I don’t have money for that.”

“I think everyone here knows and the families know there’s been a historic underinvestment in aviation,” Duffy said. “And so when the numbers come in and I put everything to the Senate and the House, they have to make a decision, what do they want to do?”

articles.body:
Kalshi has halted markets allowing users to trade on what President Trump might say on specific dates in response to an order by a federal regulator.

The prediction market platform said the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) issued an order on Friday to pause Trump-related mention markets, and the company is “complying with the order.”

In a September advisory, the agency warned such markets “present a heightened risk of manipulation,” noting they turn on “the discrete conduct of a person that may be neither independently generated nor externally verifiable.”

Mention markets allow users to place bets on whether someone will say a specific word or phrase. They came under scrutiny earlier this year when a White House teleprompter operator was fined for placing bets on the president’s speeches.

The White House suspended longtime teleprompter operator Gabriel Perez in July after Kalshi flagged suspicious trades to regulators.

Perez, who no longer works for the federal government, was accused of using his knowledge of Trump’s speeches to make more than $100,000 on mention markets.

This came on the heels of a series of other insider trading incidents involving prediction markets.

A U.S. Army official who was involved in the planning of the Venezuela raid was arrested in April for allegedly making more than $400,000 in profits from wagers on Polymarket.

articles.title: What to know about Iran’s ‘dirty bomb’ threat
articles.summary: A reported Iranian plot to carry out an alleged “dirty bomb” attack in Washington, D.C., is raising questions over potential targets, the danger of such a weapon and whether Iran even has the capability or intent to carry out that type of attack. CNN reported Monday that U.S. intelligence indicates Tehran is developing plans to…
articles.body:
A reported Iranian plot to carry out an alleged “dirty bomb” attack in Washington, D.C., is raising questions over potential targets, the danger of such a weapon and whether Iran even has the capability or intent to carry out that type of attack.

CNN reported Monday that U.S. intelligence indicates Tehran is developing plans to target senior Trump administration officials by detonating such a chemical weapon, with specific locations and targets setting off contingency planning, two sources told the outlet.

The news comes as diplomatic talks to end the nearly nine-month conflict have appeared to stall yet again, even as President Trump insists that the war is essentially over.

Washington’s intelligence apparatus reportedly picked up Iranian claims it has stashed bomb-making materials inside the United States — a process that is considered relatively easy.

The planning is currently seen as the regime giving itself options as the war stretches on, and not an indicator of an imminent attack, sources familiar with the latest intelligence told CNN.

Another line of intelligence suggests Tehran may use chemical weapons against U.S. service members, diplomatic and intelligence personnel stationed in the Middle East, as first reported by The New York Times.

A dirty bomb, which mixes conventional explosives with radioactive material, is intended to spread radioactive contamination and is seen as more effective at harming individuals in dense urban environments. Washington, the nation’s capital, is home to nearly 700,000 people in addition to tens of thousands more who come into the city daily for work.

The United States is seen as particularly vulnerable to such an attack, given that a dirty bomb is relatively easy to assemble and does not necessarily require someone to enter the country to detonate it. A person already living inside the United States could be recruited to carry out an Iranian plot.

The White House in a statement to CNN said that the U.S. is “monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland.”

Asked Tuesday about the report, President Trump said officials were taking the threat seriously and that Iran would “pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before” if it attacked Washington.

“I hope it’s not, but we take it very seriously, because they happen to be crazy,” Trump said at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila, Philippines.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin also sought to assure that “the homeland is secure,” saying on CNBC’s “Squawk Box” that Iran’s planning was “aspirational,” and not a “new threat” even as officials are taking it seriously.

“The homeland is secure, I can tell you that. But every day we are addressing new threats,” he said.

He added that any Iranian attack on the homeland “would cause an all-out war” with the U.S.

“That means we are going to use all the resources, not air resources, but all the resources to go in and destroy you,” Mullin said.

Iran has staunchly denied the report, with Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei on Tuesday calling the allegations “baseless” and a “fabricated media narrative” in a post on social platform X .

“Those who initiated the aggression against Iran are now seeking to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs by manufacturing and disseminating baseless allegations,” Baghaei wrote. “Step by step, they are attempting to manufacture a veneer of legitimacy for further aggression and atrocities.”

He added: “Iran knows well how to respond to any act of aggression and ensure that it is met with an unforgettable response.”

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi likewise on Tuesday called the report “Iraq War-style propaganda,” referring to the U.S. claims of “weapons of mass destruction” in Iraq as justification for the 2003 war.

While a dirty bomb, also known as a “radiological dispersal device” (RDD), is considered far, far less damaging than a conventional nuclear bomb, the explosion of such a weapon could cause death or injury to anyone within the blast radius.

The Nuclear Regulatory Commission says most RDDs “would not release enough radiation to kill people or cause severe illness,” but its explosion “could create fear and panic, contaminate property and require potentially costly cleanup.”

And while a dirty bomb’s radiation could be dispersed within a few blocks or miles of the explosion, it is not considered a “weapon of mass destruction,” rather a “weapon of mass disruption,” where contamination and anxiety are the main objectives, according to the commission.

(AP Photo/Vahid Salemi)

articles.title: Skepticism grows within GOP over tech failures: ‘Americans aren’t stupid’
articles.summary: Republican lawmakers and other prominent conservatives have grown skeptical over a wave of recent technology outages and failures in recent days, as some Americans stockpile canned foods and bottled water amid several high-profile outages. “Americans aren’t stupid. We want and deserve to know what’s really going on,” Tricia McLaughlin, former deputy assistant secretary for the…
articles.body:
Republican lawmakers and other prominent conservatives have grown skeptical over a wave of recent technology outages and failures in recent days, as some Americans stockpile canned foods and bottled water amid several high-profile outages .

“Americans aren’t stupid. We want and deserve to know what’s really going on,” Tricia McLaughlin, former deputy assistant secretary for the Department of Homeland Security, wrote Tuesday on the social platform X .

The latest outages to hit businesses occurred Tuesday, with Apple, Gmail and Marriott each affected, NBC 4 Washington and its affiliates reported. Sources told CNN that the National Security Agency’s (NSA) internal communications network was also down but said nothing indicated it was caused by a cyberattack.

Officials have pointed to problems with technology likely causing issues up until Tuesday, but it has opened a wave of criticism after so many outages within a short timeframe.

“Given today’s cyberattack, coupled with the [Federal Aviation Administration] ground-stops, banking failures, and Microsoft outage, it’s imperative the administration immediately brief Congress on the exact nature of the problem, so that we can have an all of government response,” Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) wrote on X on Tuesday.

“While some of this may be coincidental, it is clear we must take cybersecurity and the nefarious use of AI seriously — and act without delay,” he added.

On Monday, J.P. Morgan Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo saw disruptions preventing customers from accessing their bank accounts. United Airlines experienced a system outage also on Monday that resolved later in the evening.

The FAA implemented a nationwide ground stop last Friday, the third in the agency’s history, believed by investigators to have been caused by a router needing an upgrade at a radio facility in Arkansas. And last Thursday, a global outage affected 100,000 Microsoft users and cut off access to Outlook and other Office apps like Teams.

Other lawmakers echoed Lawler’s sentiment, including Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.), who told reporters that if “this is all a coincidence, it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.”

“Five major outages in less than a week. Microsoft. Workday. The FAA. Major banks. Now the NSA’s classified communications network. Congress needs to be briefed immediately. The American people deserve answers about what’s going on,” Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) wrote on X .

Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) told TMZ that his opinion on the outages “are the results of hackers,” but he was unsure if these potential hacks were “coordinated,” only that “these are not coincidences.” He speculated that rogue AI could be a perpetrator.

“I’m not suggesting we don’t need AI or AI’s bad or AI’s an ignorant slut or any of that,” Kennedy told the outlet. “But AI certainly makes it easier to hack, and I think that’s what you’re seeing going on.”

Kennedy also called on intelligence agencies to inform Congress “what’s going on.”

Far-right influencer Laura Loomer claimed on X that all of the outages are what intelligence officials call “signaling,” or a type of “pre-warning before a major hack or debilitating cyber attack,” according to a source.

“Source told me this is likely the work of Iran with assistance from China and or Russia, whose hackers they tell me are more sophisticated than the Iranians,” she wrote.

Some noteworthy voices on the right have called on the White House to respond to what has happened. Former press secretary Karoline Leavitt said she is “wondering the same thing” about the frequency in which these outages have occurred.

“I’m checking my bank account with a little bit of worry,” she told Fox News.” And what I would say to the White House is transparency is key.”

Meghan McCain, daughter of former Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) urged that someone “high in the [Trump] administration needs to get on tv and tell the American people NOW what is going on,” an X post from her read .

The administration has approached these incidents differently, with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy calling on increased funding from Congress to go toward refurbishing the FAA’s infrastructure. But in response to the outages as a whole, President Trump said, “ It’s fine .”

Vice President Vance told Fox News’s Laura Ingraham Monday that the White House does not “see a crisis coming down,” and said friends have asked if “they should prepare to build a bunker or stock up on food and water.”

“My answer to that is no,” Vance continued. “We don’t see a crisis coming down. But you have to be prepared for everything.”

Leavitt referred to these comments in her interview with the same outlet and said the White House should take that message “wide and loud” to the public “to really calm the temperature.”

This extends to alerting Congress, as House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) requested the administration to brief Congress on the outages. He said Tuesday that he’s talked with Duffy but that he came away without a path for how Congress should respond, calling the rash of incidents “troubling.”

“And it’s unclear if it’s all infrastructure related, or whether there’s some malignant activity,” Jeffries said at a press briefing, adding that having the administration and Congress meet will help lawmakers “be informed about the steps that need to be taken, and we can inform the people of the United States of America.”

articles.title: Democrats try to figure out how not to get swept away by the blue wave
articles.summary: At What’s Next, a post-midterms conference funded by a billionaire AI investor, a group of centrist Democrats aims to harness the populist moment.
articles.body: On a harried Saturday afternoon at Denver International Airport, I had the good fortune of sitting just a few feet from Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey. It shouldn’t have come as a surprise. He, I, and 3,500 or so others had just left “What’s Next,” a conference organized by Majority Democrats, a group dedicated to charting a path for the suddenly — and shockingly? — victorious party. Frey, who rose to national prominence amid ICE’s brutal Operation Metro Surge, had come to the conference in Denver to listen, not to speak. “I’ve never been to one of these things before,” he said. He had flown in for a day and, like everyone else in attendance, is curious to see where the party goes from here. He said he hopes Democrats do two things with their newfound power. “One, act with urgency. And second, don’t fuck it up.” Another conference-goer sitting nearby chimed in: “Abso-fucking-lutely.” Democrats, unaccustomed to winning, have seemingly learned from the folly of Republicans’ 2024 sweep. Where Donald Trump’s return to power was falsely attributed to a vibe shift of seismic proportions, born of voters’ preoccupation over DEI and desire to say slurs, Majority Democrats has a simpler explanation for the blue tsunami: It’s the economy, stupid. Everything is falling apart, and even just getting by feels more expensive than ever. The midterms were a rejection, not an endorsement: Voters rejected data centers, they rejected war, and they cast their lot with the side that promised to give them what they want. The Democrats understand this is not a cultural victory. Even the hollow center of the Democratic Party has, at long last, realized voters don’t necessarily want what they’re selling — they just want to afford to live. It’s gas and groceries all the way down. This analysis would almost verge on Marxist if it wasn’t put forth by an organization comprising the party’s new, young moderates. Majority Democrats describes itself as an alternative to three unpopular, ineffective factions: the “gerontocratic establishment,” the “activist left,” and the “MAGA right.” The Democrats want you to know they’ve changed. This is no longer the party of “Kamala is brat” or “Pokémon Go to the polls.” They are, in fact, “A Different Kind of Democrat.” They’ve abandoned hollow identity politics and sworn off toxic factional infighting. They really, really care about affordability — for real. They even have the merch to prove it. Attendees at What’s Next wore their convictions on their sleeves, and also their chests, and also their heads. There were hats that read “pay your taxes” and hats identifying the wearer as a “new deal democrat,” both in all lowercase because the Democrats would also like to remind you that they are once again the youth party. At a separate merch stand, there was a T-shirt declaring “America!” and another T-shirt posing an existential question, also in all lowercase: “how did fucking computers become the thing and machines became the thing that does art? and humans are like the ones in amazon warehouses like shouldn’t robots be working so we can paint?” This second shirt, a friend pointed out, is an uncredited reference to a joke alt-comedian Stavros Halkias made on Theo Von’s podcast. And there was the Our Get Along Shirt, a sartorial exercise in magical thinking that summed up the ethos of the What’s Next conference. The Democrats were in control. Having realized the folly of fighting each other, they would instead channel their energy into fighting for the American people. [Media: The illusion of harmony was shattered early into the programming when a small group of dissenters heckled Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the soon-to-be speaker of the House. “We’re asking you to listen to us now,” one of the protesters shouted after the moderator, Fox News’s resident Democratic host Jessica Tarlov, attempted to placate them by saying she’d be asking Jeffries about the youth vote. “When is the time for a Green New Deal? When is the time for an arms embargo?” The protesters’ cries were drowned out by the crowd’s chants of “HA-KEEM, HA-KEEM, HA-KEEM.” Jeffries, ever the politician, was unfazed by the altercation. “I’m from Brooklyn,” he told his visibly uncomfortable interlocutor. “This is light work.” The protesters were whisked away, and the interview continued as if the interruption had never happened. Democrats would be gracious in victory. This new way of doing things was best summed up by Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who told reporters that she and her new colleague, Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, had plenty of debates in the car en route to campaign events — though she declined to say what the debates were about. (Slotkin has identified as a Zionist but has also voted against providing certain military aid to Israel. El-Sayed has called Israel’s war on Gaza a genocide.) “Abdul and I do not agree on everything, but we agree on the really big, important thing, and that is making sure we have a middle class in this country,” she said. “When I see elected officials spending their time fighting the progressive-versus-moderate battle, I know that person didn’t actually learn a damn thing from the election.” Throughout the weekend, speaker after speaker urged Democrats not to squander their newfound control of Congress by bickering among themselves. At the airport, notorious Democratic operative Lis Smith, an adviser to Majority Democrats, told me the midterms sweep was a rejection of Trumpism, not a sign that voters prefer one style of Democratic politics over the other. “A big takeaway of the election was that there’s no one way to be a Democrat, and that’s in part how we were able to have such a big victory,” she said. The calls for unity were reminiscent of the slogan of one doomed 2016 presidential campaign: Stronger Together. This time, however, they may be onto something — at least for now. “It’s easy to have Pete Buttigieg and Ro Khanna onstage when we’re all riding the same high,” one staffer told me on the final night of the conference. But what happens when it’s actually time to govern? [Image: Audience members are escorted out as they yell at Minority Leader of the U.S House of Representatives Hakeem Jeffries, speaks with Moderator Jessica Tarlov. For all the talk of unity, there was plenty of tension at What’s Next — sometimes overt, more often simmering beneath the surface of what organizers described as a congenial event. There was tension toward the establishment, as characterized by Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s announcement that he was challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-NY) for Senate majority leader. There was tension between speakers’ repeated exhortations to get “big money” out of politics and the fact that Majority Democrats is largely bankrolled by hedge fund billionaire Stephen Mandel, a major investor in companies powering the AI boom. (Several attendees I spoke to described What’s Next as hands down the most luxe Democratic event they’ve been to, on par with the party’s national conventions. The snack station was stocked with full-size candy bars.) There was tension between all the populist posturing and the nightly afterparties at the Ritz, where 2028 contenders, staffers, and hangers-on of all types drank well after last call. And notwithstanding the recent blue tsunami, there was tension between Democrats’ persistent unlikability and the conference’s poptimism-tinged branding. Everything was a little too cute. Majority Democrats staffers wore custom Dickies-style jackets with their names embroidered on the front. Highlight reels played between each main stage speech. The opening-night happy hour, sponsored by the Searchlight Institute — a think tank founded in 2025 with the stated goal of weakening the influence of liberal groups like the ACLU and the Center for American Progress — was Western-themed, though hardly any attendees strayed from the blazer-and-lanyard dress code that is de rigueur in liberal policy circles. The conference lineup was announced via a music festival-style flyer. The halls were decorated with stylized posters of the politicians in attendance, many of whom seemed to be soft-launching their 2028 presidential campaigns. “The organizers here want a big tent — one big enough even to invite anti-establishment voices like me,” Khanna, one apparent presidential aspirant, said from the stage. “I’m all for a big tent. I’m not for a shallow one. A big tent cannot mean that we water down principle for political expediency.” He called on the new Democratic-controlled Congress to pass Medicare for All, codify a path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants, abolish ICE, and cut off funding to Israel, which he said was committing an ongoing genocide against Palestinians. All of this got huge cheers from the audience — some of whom, one presumes, also applauded Jeffries just one day earlier. Depending on whom you ask, What’s Next was either a concerted effort to rally Democrats around an affordability agenda or moderates’ cynical attempt at co-opting voters’ populist rage. Across the street from the Mission Ballroom, a small group of protesters with Indivisible unfurled a giant banner that read “NO SCHUMER CORONATION.” Members of another group, posted up by one of the side stages hosting the “Do Issues Matter?” panel, told me they hoped the Democrats didn’t abandon their commitment to immigration reform and abortion rights. At the “AI safety breakfast,” one advocate of tech regulation told me there was little daylight between the organizations putting on the conference and its affiliated events — Majority Democrats, the Searchlight Institute, and the pro-AI regulation PAC Tomorrow Together — and the flailing Abundance movement. “They’re rebranding because no one likes abundance,” she said. “This is counter-programming to the populist left. They took a bunch of AI safety money to put on things like this.” There were notable absences. Vermont senator and erstwhile presidential candidate Bernie Sanders was not in attendance, and neither was New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, whom the New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America recently urged to run for president. Slotkin may have name-checked El-Sayed, but he wasn’t there, either. Not even Colorado Rep.-elect Melat Kiros – a member of the Democratic Socialists of America who won her race in a landslide and now represents the very district where the conference was held – was present. Rep. Jake Auchincloss, a member of Majority Democrats who helped organize the event, told The Washington Post that he had personally invited Ocasio-Cortez. [Image: What’s Next seemingly wants to make Democrats cool again. Still, there were other representatives of the party’s left wing milling about, including Khanna, Van Hollen, and Angie Nixon, a DSA-backed Democrat who came within 3 percentage points of winning a Florida Senate seat. And regardless of their political leanings — and counter to the Democratic Party’s 2024 message that the economy was just fine, actually — nearly every single speaker decried the steadily increasing economic divide separating America’s billionaires from the shrinking middle class and the growing ranks of the working poor. “We just won in a historic fashion, and I think everyone feels good about that,” said Morris Katz, a 26-year-old digital strategist whose roster of previous clients includes New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa. (Katz was also the driving force behind Senate contender Graham Platner, who dropped out of the race after being accused of sexual assault.) “I think everyone is united under an anti-billionaire focus on affordability and corruption, and there’s a lot to feel good about.” And what about the billionaire funding this very conference? “If there are people who want to support where we’re headed, and the things we’re doing, great, everyone’s welcome,” Katz told me. The difference, he said, is whether Democrats let themselves be co-opted or corrupted by their donors. He pointed to outgoing Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott — who supercharged tech development in the state and whose campaign was largely funded by Elon Musk and data center developers — as an example of what could go wrong. “There’s a quid pro quo there that needs to be avoided at all costs. We need to be the anti-Big Tech party.” Democrats are already heading in that direction. Khanna pointed out that one-third of the nation’s wealth is concentrated in the Silicon Valley district he represents. Jerusalem Demsas, founder of the liberal publication The Argument, urged legislators to rein in AI development. (“I know everyone here is in a good mood, and it’s about to not be a good mood,” she said before reminding the assembled legislators and political operatives that “what comes after winning is governing.”) At a press conference after her speech, Slotkin called for the establishment of a bipartisan, bicameral committee on AI akin to midcentury bodies created to regulate nuclear power. “While we’re bickering with each other — Democrats and Republicans — there’s an opportunity cost, and we have not done what we need to do on AI,” she said. “If we were healthy politically, we would have been working on this for five years straight.” There was an obvious undercurrent of technopessimism throughout the weekend. News of the nationwide FAA ground stop broke minutes before a panel titled “How Weird Will AI Make 2028?” Though a faulty router was ultimately identified as the culprit, attendees — myself included — couldn’t help but speculate whether an AI cyberattack, or even just shoddy implementation of the FAA’s new AI tool, was actually to blame. “It was clear that there is just a huge interest in AI here, and grappling with it, that sits across the party,” Rob Flaherty, the cofounder of the AI safety PAC Tomorrow Together told me. Flaherty’s organization hosted an off-the-record breakfast on AI safety. “We built it for 100 people, and 600 people showed up,” he said. The coffee ran out almost immediately, though there were somehow enough burritos to go around. Tomorrow Together’s polling, which was shared at the breakfast, indicates that voters don’t just hate data centers but have broadly soured on AI. They tie AI developments to broader economic concerns like rising utility bills and a worsening job market. Most importantly, voters don’t think the companies can be trusted to regulate themselves. “Now it’s on Democrats to not just channel the anger and be the vessel for that anger but to actually enact the things that are going to alleviate the pain that people are feeling,” Flaherty told me. But for Flaherty, who previously worked for Biden’s and Harris’ presidential campaigns, the conference “was less about a policy agenda and more about a theory of power” — one articulated by Bernie Sanders a decade ago. “If you look at the way people — James Talarico on down, Hakeem Jeffries on down — were speaking, it doesn’t sound dissimilar from the kinds of things Bernie was raising in 2016,” said Flaherty. “He rightly — and I was working on the other side — identified some of the economic discontent that a lot of people are feeling.” [Image: Stylized posters of the assembled politicians and operatives were everywhere. A poster of Searchlight Institute founder Adam Jentleson (not pictured) hung above a urinal in the men’s room. Still, there’s a difference between Sanders’ vision of Medicare for All and, say, a public option — or what 2020 presidential hopeful Pete Buttigieg described as “Medicare for all who want it.” Both fall under the broad umbrella of universal healthcare, but the distinctions matter. Absent nitty-gritty policy discussions, however, it’s easy to get the sense that all voters — and all Democrats — want the same thing. Perhaps this is why, even among the professional Democrats in attendance, I met people who told me they wanted Democrats to prosecute ICE agents, enact a $25 an hour minimum wage, and pack the Supreme Court. At a certain point, I became desperate to find someone whose politics were a little more tepid. My pleas were answered by Uriel Espinoza, a local Democrat whose friends introduced him as a centrist. Espinoza’s friends insisted that I join them for happy hour at a nearby brewery. (Espinoza said he rejects the centrist label, but broadly disagrees with the Democratic Socialists of America’s manifesto.) Their car wasn’t big enough to fit us all, but it didn’t matter. As four of us piled into the back seat of a Tesla whose driver — another member of the friend group — was blasting Drake, Espinoza told me he had once identified as a conservative. At the bar, he and another friend said the conference had been fun, if a little “East Coast consultant-y.” Here was the mythical moderate voter in all his glory. He was even wearing a cowboy hat. And what did he want? Immigration reform, universal healthcare, and an economy that isn’t stacked against working people. There was a time, Espinoza told me, when he felt betrayed. “On certain things — like Israel, Gaza, Palestine, immigration — we are looking to our elected officials at the highest level, and we feel that they aren’t really delivering, or differentiating himself from Republicans,” he said. I told him he sounded almost like a leftist. “I’m also surprised, myself, because I’ve never thought of myself — and I don’t think of myself — as a socialist,” he told me. “I’m an entrepreneur. I’m pro-business, I’m pro-economy, but I’m also, at this point, pro-results.” Update, November 17th: This piece has been updated to include Uriel Espinoza’s description of his political leanings.

articles.title: New York Fed's Williams rules out jumbo rate hike for December
articles.summary: "I don't think the situation calls for dramatic action," Williams said Tuesday.
articles.body:
New York Federal Reserve president John Williams poured cold water on the central bank making a jumbo 50-basis-point interest rate hike next month but noted that the Fed does have to get inflation down.

"I don't think the situation calls for dramatic action," Williams said during a Q&A with Axios in New York.

Williams acknowledged that the data is sending a "pretty clear signal."

"We still have our work to do to make sure that we bring inflation back down to 2% in a timely way and in a sustained manner," he said.

Williams' comments come as the latest inflation data shows price growth that is surprisingly higher than expected. The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% in October , compared with expectations of 0.3%, marking a slight cooldown from September's 0.6% gain. "Core" inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3%, compared with expectations of 0.2% and unchanged from September.

A reading of the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge showed prices heated up in September, with the core Personal Consumption Expenditures index rising 3.1% , up a tenth of a percentage point from 3% in August.

Markets have been weighing a larger rate hike ever since inflation readings came in hot. Fed governor Chris Waller said ahead of the CPI report that if consumer prices were higher than expected, he'd consider a move of 50 basis points.

After Williams spoke on Tuesday, investors still saw a 98% chance the Fed hikes by 25 basis points in December.

Williams wouldn't characterize inflation as broadening, but acknowledged a continuation of higher price increases on imported goods where tariffs are in place and energy prices that are being passed on. He also pointed to AI investments causing certain prices, such as semiconductors, to rise. Williams identified AI as the most likely "persistent" factor of inflation.

How many rate hikes and at what pace the Fed must implement them will depend on what's happening in AI, Williams said. He noted that a lot of strength in the economy is coming from AI, and consumer spending is being boosted by a strong stock market.

"If those continue, I think that that's a factor that will argue that we may need to raise rates more at the same time those factors have been pushing inflation up. But there's just a great deal of uncertainty," he said.

Follow Jennifer Schonberger on X @Jenniferisms and on Instagram .

articles.title: Trump nominates new Army chief of staff after Hegseth’s April ouster
articles.summary: President Trump formally nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve to be the Army’s new chief of staff on Tuesday, nine months after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired his predecessor, Gen. Randy George. “GEN Christopher LaNeve is an exceptional leader who has commanded at every echelon of the Army. He knows exactly what it takes to build a…
articles.body:
President Trump formally nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve to be the Army’s new chief of staff on Tuesday, nine months after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired his predecessor , Gen. Randy George.

“GEN Christopher LaNeve is an exceptional leader who has commanded at every echelon of the Army. He knows exactly what it takes to build a force that can fight and win. He is the right leader at the right time to modernize the Army and ensure our Soldiers are prepared to dominate on any battlefield,” Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said in a statement . “I cannot think of anyone better to serve as our next Chief of Staff of the Army.”

Military leadership nominations are usually able to pass through the Senate easily, but LaNeve’s is sure to face backlash. The Hill previously reported that lawmakers in both parties on the Senate Armed Services Committee (SASC) expressed opposition to LaNeve, who previously served as Hegseth’s senior military assistant.

Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.), who sits on SASC, told The Hill in August that he had heard from some on the panel who felt LaNeve “doesn’t have enough four-star experience.”

If LaNeve was confirmed, it would mark a rapid ascension during his time in the Army. He has served since the 1990’s, when he was commissioned into the infantry. He previously was commander of the 82nd Airborne Division at Fort Bragg, N.C., before heading the Eighth Army in South Korea as a three-star general.

LaNeve is also serving as the Army’s vice chief of staff. On Tuesday, the administration nominated Lt. Gen. Marcus S. Evans for the role.

Telle on Tuesday praised Evans as “relentless in his commitment to building a more ready and lethal force. He is a proven leader who knows what our Soldiers need to succeed.”

Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa), who served in the Army Reserve and the Iowa Army National Guard, has expressed objections to LaNeve’s nomination.

“Certainly if LaNeve is brought up, I think there would be a number of folks that would block him, because it’s not just the issue of Randy George. It’s it is much much broader than that,” a Senate Republican source told The Hill in late September.

George, the previous chief of staff, was confirmed by the Senate in 2023 after being nominated by former President Joe Biden. He was purged from the Army amid the firings of dozens of other senior military officers, including Air Force Vice Chief of Staff Gen. James Slife, the head of the Defense Intelligence Agency, Lt. Gen. Jeffrey Kruse and Chief of Naval Operations, Adm. Lisa Franchetti.

articles.title: Google joins the tech outage trend by announcing it's not having one | TechCrunch
articles.summary: With tech outages seemingly everywhere, Google took the unusual step of announcing that Gmail is working just fine, actually.
articles.body:
Was Google feeling a little left out of the recent wave of tech outages? The company took to X on Tuesday to announce that its Gmail service is actually running just fine. In a post, the company said it was not currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption and reminded users they could always check Gmail’s real-time status on its online dashboard .

As it turns out, the company was trying to head off reports of a Gmail outage that began circulating on X on Tuesday around the same time that Apple was seeing a number of verified outages of its own . While some posts on the social network suggested Gmail was experiencing a disruption, others said they were not having any problems.

The concerns seemed to stem from an X post by Downdetector, a crowdsourced website where users can report service disruptions themselves and see if others are having problems. Downdetector is not an official source for verifying or understanding the true scope of internet outages, and as people become more concerned about possible cyberattacks, the site’s data may become less valuable over time if every minor glitch and hiccup is reported as an “outage” by non-technical users.

The fact that Google had to announce it was not having an outage speaks to the growing anxiety around the reliability of major tech services. Over the past week, Apple and Microsoft experienced outages, an FAA network failure led to a nationwide ground stop, and some banks and airlines also reported disruptions.

However, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Fox Business Tuesday that the U.S. is not currently facing coordinated cyberattacks. He told the outlet, “We do not see the indicia of a coordinated cyberattack — let me just be clear about that — and we do not see the indicia of state-sponsored activity here.”

Instead, Clayton attributed the rise in issues to businesses patching their systems. The patching may be a downstream effect of AI, as newer models have become increasingly adept at uncovering previously unknown vulnerabilities. “They’re upgrading them, they’re putting patches in place,” he said, adding that this is happening at “a much larger scale” than before.

As a result, some of the systems are “not coming back as expected in all cases,” he added.

articles.title: Hung Cao grilled by Senate over suicide attempts, Iran war: 5 takeaways
articles.summary: Senators on both sides of the aisle grilled acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao on Tuesday with questions over sailor suicide attempts on Navy ships, the U.S. war against Iran and the lack of progress on shipbuilding in a contentious two-and-a-half-hour confirmation hearing. Senate Armed Services Committee (SASC) lawmakers berated the Pentagon for holding some classified…
articles.body:
Senators on both sides of the aisle grilled acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao on Tuesday with questions over sailor suicide attempts on Navy ships, the U.S. war against Iran and the lack of progress on shipbuilding in a contentious two-and-a-half-hour confirmation hearing.

Senate Armed Services Committee (SASC) lawmakers berated the Pentagon for holding some classified briefings with only Republicans in the room and pressed Cao, who has been serving in the acting role since April, over President Trump’s memo directing the Navy to replace Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System (EMALS) with traditional steam catapults on aircraft carriers.

Democrats also challenged Cao over prolonged Navy ship deployments and their impact on sailors’ mental health, as well as what he has advised Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to do to help end the conflict in the Middle East.

If confirmed, Cao said he is prepared to work with all senators to instill “necessary” changes through three priorities: “take care of our sailors and marines, advance shipbuilding initiatives and defend our homeland.”

The acting Navy secretary’s nomination also requires a congressional waiver because he’s not been out of active-duty service for the seven years required by federal law.

Grilled on suicide attempts on Navy ships

Senators questioned Cao over grueling conditions on Navy ships, which have led to suicide attempts and a debilitating mental health situation amid the war with Iran.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) said lawmakers were very familiar with problems from the lengthy deploymen t of the USS Abraham Lincoln .

“You’re failing these sailors and their families, and your confrontation with them leaves me with the clear impression that you simply don’t care,” Blumenthal told Cao. “But equally important, you failed to provide Congress with a full and transparent accounting of the toll on these sailors and their families.”

Cao said he cares “greatly” for the sailors and looks at everything through one lens only: how will it affect his son, who is in the Marines. The acting Navy secretary added that he does not control deployment lengths.

Cao told Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.) in September that eight sailors assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during a lengthy deployment

Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), a former Navy pilot, said his office is hearing concerns about conditions aboard the USS George Washington and the Boxer Amphibious Ready Group.

“One parent told us that their kid lost more than 45 pounds in six months because of a lack of food, but also lacked basic hygiene supplies. Another reported significant weight loss among Marines, some visibly malnourished,” Kelly said before later asking Cao what the Navy is doing to make sure sailors are supported during extended deployments.

The most contentious part of the hearing came during Gillibrand’s line of questioning, when Cao confirmed he put out a statement calling news reports about grueling conditions aboard USS Abraham Lincoln “dishonest.”

“I did, Senator, and I spoke to our sailors on board, and they felt the same way,” he said.

Gillibrand then referenced the letter she received from Cao about eight suicide attempts on the Lincoln strike group and asked “were the president and Secretary Hegseth wrong to dismiss those concerns?”

“Well, Senator, again, these are eight mitigations we’re able to mitigate,” Cao said before the New York senator erupted.

“Please don’t call attempted suicide mitigations. That is such an insult. It’s an insult to these men and women who are devoting their lives to the armed services. When you say it’s mitigation, you’re compartmentalizing something that is clearly a mental health failure,” she said in a heightened tone. “The fact that a service member, a sailor, went overboard is beyond a mitigation.”

“Senator, that sailor was not trying to kill himself, and he admitted that,” Cao said before Gillibrand interrupted “What was he trying to do? Swim to Guam?”

The acting Navy secretary said the jump did not result in a death and the sailor leaped with a life preserver on.

“Maybe to save whatever discipline he was about to undergo. But I think you are minimizing what mental health strain is on these service members,” Gillibrand replied before calling for a separate hearing focused on sailors’ mental health.

Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), a former Black Hawk helicopter pilot, repeatedly asked Cao if he urged Hegseth to end the Iran war over impacts on Navy readiness.

Cao said Hegseth “knows my stance on our readiness and the strain it takes on our sailors” before Duckworth cut him off.

“I cannot vote for you because you’re going to be another yes-man,” she said.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) questioned Cao about how much it cost the Navy to enforce the naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz .

“I do not know the daily cost, ma’am,” he said.

Warren then said an independent estimate put the figure at about $32.5 million per day, asking Cao if the number sounds right.

“Let me do some quick Asian math in my head. But yes, it’s about 30 billion dollars,” Cao replied.

When Warren asked how much damage Iranian strikes inflicted on the U.S. base in Bahrain, which is home to the Navy’s Fifth Fleet , Cao did not provide a number.

“We have not been able to do a full assessment yet,” he said, adding it is a non-permissive area for us to go.”

Cao also clashed with Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), a former CIA analyst and Pentagon official, over who controls the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb. Cao said the U.S. does.

But when Slotkin asked if a commercial ship can transit those two points without a U.S. military escort, Cao said “no, Senator, they haven’t been able to do that even before the war.”

When Slotkin asked if a year ago the same commercial vessels needed a military escort, Cao said “Senator, that’s why their insurance rates is $54,000 just in one transit…it’s so dangerous over there, Senator.”

“You’re dodging the question,” Slotkin said. “A year ago today, a commercial ship flagged for any nation could successfully transit the Bab el-Mandeb and the Strait of Hormuz without a naval escort.”

Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), who said he recently visited the USS Gerald R. Ford, asked if the Navy should return to using steam systems to launch aircraft off aircraft carriers, as directed in an August memo from President Trump.

“The whole question is how can I maintain 11 carriers at this point because of the delays with EMALS and the electromagnetic elevators. It’s delaying our carriers by seven years. We’re going to have five years where we’re going to be down to nine carriers,” Cao said.

Kaine, who beat Cao during his 2024 Senate election bid, then asked if Cao is considering returning to steam launches.

Cao began discussing elevators, which lift up the jets to the carrier’s deck, before Kaine cut him off, saying he did not ask about those and praised the EMALS, which experts said are a superior option.

After Kaine concluded his round of questions, Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), the chairman of SASC, chimed in with an ultimatum: “Returning to steam is a nonstarter, and everyone needs to understand that.”

GOP unhappy about classified briefings without Democrats

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said there have been “multiple occasions” this year where his Democratic colleagues were not invited for classified briefings on defense programs, saying it is hard to build bipartisan support for the Pentagon’s budget when they are not even in the room.

Rounds asked Cao for a commitment to have both parties in future briefings.

“If confirmed, I will. I commit to being open and honest with the entire Senate and the Congress . Also, I mean, this is a bipartisan issue,” he told Rounds. “National defense is not a partisan issue.”

The frustrations came from Democrats as well.

“I’m deeply concerned that there are briefings with Republicans only on our national security in classified settings that Democrats aren’t invited to. That has to end today,” Gillibrand said.

Kaine pointed to the frustrations the committee has had with obtaining timely information from the Pentagon in the past two years.

“And you come into the hearing a little bit under a shadow, not of your own making, because I think that many on the dais in both parties have not been happy with the responsiveness of the Pentagon to requests for information,” he said.

Pressure over the firings on the USS South Dakota

Sen. Jack Reed (D-R.I.), the top Democrat on the panel, lambasted Cao for not notifying Congress of the firing of the three leaders of a Navy Virginia-class attack submarine USS South Dakota.

“We need to have details promptly, and you have to do that, and you didn’t do it,” Reed said before asking Cao to explain what transpired before the removal of the commanding officer, executive officer and chief of the boat of the submarine.

“There was a near-mishap issue, and we’re still investigating it,” Cao said. “However, the squadron commodore felt that they did not live up to their honor, courage and commitment ethos.”

Cao justified withholding details, some of which surfaced last week in news reports , to protect the privacy and career prospects of those officers.

“Why did you not bring this to the attention of Congress in the way that had been done in the past,” Kaine later asked.

“My answer is there’s no excuse, Senator. I will. I spoke to [Rep. Joe] Courtney [D-Conn.] in depth about this. We will come up with procedures so I can inform you on a timely manner,” Gao said. “My thing is I just didn’t want it to be blasted out on Navy Times.”

articles.title: Nvidia says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
articles.summary: Nvidia’s Q3 2027 earnings call started by saying the board does not intend to reinstate former CEO Jensen Huang and would not take questions on his resignation.
articles.body: Starting Nvidia’s quarterly earnings call on Tuesday, new board chair Harvey Jones said that when former CEO Jensen Huang resigned, “the Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” Jones added, “We will not be addressing or taking questions on today’s call regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation.” Huang had publicly floated the idea of returning earlier on Tuesday. In a statement posted to X, he wrote that he “did not live up to the standards expected of everyone” at the company, that he regretted his mistakes, and that he would cooperate with the Nvidia board’s investigation into his actions. He added that he’d be willing to return to the chief executive role if offered it, though a day earlier, the Nvidia board reportedly said it was not considering bringing him back. “NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company,” Huang wrote. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” But since his November 12th resignation, Huang remains entangled in scandal. He’s reportedly had three affairs, two with subordinates at Nvidia, one with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset suspected of facilitating illicit chip sales. (Huang has pushed against restrictions on Nvidia chip sales in China.) He’s scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1st, and an internal company investigation is ongoing. Tech industry heavyweights have still voiced their support for Huang, dubbing him “irreplaceable” and petitioning for his return. Some have cast doubt on the allegations that Alice Huang (no relation) was spying on behalf of China and painted the leaks about their relationship as a conspiracy against the former CEO. President Donald Trump, a close ally of Huang for much of the past year, has also backed him. On Monday, Trump said he “would not mind” Huang returning, adding that “I think he learned a big lesson — I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another.” Trump’s closeness with Huang could also complicate things for Nvidia, however. The company has ramped up its lobbying in Washington, D.C., spending $5 million in 2025 and $4.7 million so far in 2026. But as Democrats prepare to take Congress, they’re planning to investigate Trump’s dealings with Big Tech and other industries, alleging potential corruption. “The election wasn’t very positive for AI, and [the news around Huang’s resignation] is only going to complicate things, especially for the company in particular but for AI as a whole going forward,” Brendan Glavin, director of insights at OpenSecrets, told The Verge in an interview last week. Lior Prosor, managing partner at Deep33, a tech VC firm, said last week that he didn’t expect Huang’s resignation to pop the AI bubble, although Huang has had a significant hand in mobilizing funds for the AI infrastructure buildout in the U.S. Under Huang’s leadership in August, Nvidia entered into partnerships with six financial institutions for about $500 billion to fund such endeavors. “NVIDIA supplies roughly 75 percent of the AI compute hardware the industry consumes, and demand continues to dramatically outpace supply,” Deep33’s Prosor said in an interview with The Verge. “Neither its customers nor its competitors can easily replace the capabilities it provides, and the economic incentives driving the AI trade remain unchanged.” Even so, a potential market cooling has some worried, as Anthropic’s IPO, slated to potentially be the largest of all time, is set for Thursday. The chipmaker had agreed to buy $10 billion in Anthropic shares via private placement, on top of a $10 billion funding promise Nvidia had already made last year.

articles.title: Court ruling throws wrench into Trump’s bid for offshore mining
articles.summary: A court ruling this week is throwing a wrench into the Trump administration’s bid to open up mining off the coast of American Samoa. Judge Jill Otake, an appointee of President Trump, ruled that the administration did not adequately consider the potential impacts of offshore mining during its Endangered Species Act (ESA) review. Her ruling…
articles.body:
A court ruling this week is throwing a wrench into the Trump administration’s bid to open up mining off the coast of American Samoa.

Judge Jill Otake, an appointee of President Trump, ruled that the administration did not adequately consider the potential impacts of offshore mining during its Endangered Species Act (ESA) review.

Her ruling noted that the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) “only considered the preliminary effects of the lease sale and did not even attempt to consider” other activities such as actual mining.

She wrote that the agency’s “cramped, expedited, informal consultation is apparently unprecedented” and vacated the letter determining that no further ESA consultation was required for the lease sale.

The ruling does not appear to explicitly vacate the lease sale itself, however, and it’s not immediately clear whether the Trump administration will attempt to move forward with the sale, which had been scheduled for Thursday.

A spokesperson for the Marine Minerals Administration said that the agency, which would carry out the lease sale, “is aware of the opinion” in an email to The Hill. “We are currently working to address the issues raised in the court’s opinion.”

However, in a separate but related case challenging the lease sale itself rather than the review that upheld it, Otake wrote that if she vacates the review but the Trump administration moves ahead with the lease sale, “any bidders for the leases will be on notice that the Court has determined that NMFS violated the Endangered Species Act … regarding the proposed leases.”

David Henkin, an attorney with Earthjustice who is representing groups seeking to block the potential offshore mining, said that taken together, the judge’s statements are a warning to potential bidders that “if you buy those leases knowing that they haven’t complied with the Endangered Species Act, do not be surprised if the court later sets aside voids, vacates, throws into the garbage can those leases.”

Henkin also more broadly took issue with the potential mining itself, calling it a “highly speculative and risky endeavor with our oceans, on which we rely to protect us from the worst effects of global climate change, when the minerals that these companies want to bring from the bottom of the ocean are available already from terrestrial sources.”

The Trump administration has sought to advance offshore mining, announcing the American Samoa lease sale — the first of its kind — last month.

Mike Olsen, the Marine Minerals Administration’s acting director, said at the time that the U.S. needed minerals, writing in a statement: “Critical minerals are no longer just commodities; they are a vital strategic asset in global competition, essential for reaching our energy efficiency goals, strengthening our national defense, and securing domestic supply chains.”

articles.title: Director of National Intelligence offers explanation for tech outages
articles.summary: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton pushed back Tuesday on public speculation surrounding recent tech outages, attributing many to system upgrades as opposed to cyberattacks. “Let me tell you what this is not, as far as we can tell … this is not a cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation…
articles.body:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton pushed back Tuesday on public speculation surrounding recent tech outages, attributing many to system upgrades as opposed to cyberattacks.

“Let me tell you what this is not, as far as we can tell … this is not a cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation state. We’ve looked very closely,” Clayton told CNBC.

“What I think is going on here, and I think there’s both a good news aspect to this and an aspect that we need to be clear-eyed about, is many people are patching their systems,” he added. “They know that they’re legacy systems, have vulnerabilities, they’re outdated … it is time for an upgrade across our digital infrastructure.”

Clayton’s comments came as high-profile tech outages hit multiple industries within the last week — impacting flights, banking systems, email and beyond — which raised alarm bells nationwide surrounding the potential for large-scale cybersecurity breaches. And Trump administration officials were left to answer for them.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said super intelligence (SI) — the administration’s preferred term for artificial intelligence — may be the cause of the recent tech outages, citing a discussion with an unidentified member of the tech industry.

“I started talking to the tech industry,” Mullin told Fox News on Monday, adding he talked to a person in tech that thought “that it’s the SI, he said, because these programs aren’t designed to work as fast as SI is.”

“When they put in a program that’s able to write codes and it goes in, it self-fixes itself,” Mullin continued. “It’s like doing a change order on a house. When you change one thing in a house, everything else starts changing, that’s a ripple effect. And it causes a system to be overran that weren’t designed to run as fast as the SI technology is today.”

Clayton echoed Mullin’s point Tuesday, signaling that tech infrastructure “upgrades” — including the integration of AI — may have led to the recent issues.

Microsoft users across the globe last Thursday experienced widespread outages affecting platforms including Outlook and Teams. The problem lasted for about a day and was “introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” the company said after restoring the platforms.

The day after, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop, stretching on for more than four hours. Officials initially linked the incident to an overload of data on routers, with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy later saying a contractor’s telecommunications line switch caused the issue that sparked the stoppage.

articles.title: White House pulls nomination of Heidi Overton to lead FDA
articles.summary: The White House withdrew the nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) amid opposition from Senate Republicans, it confirmed to The Hill. Overton was set to face a key vote Wednesday in the Senate health committee, where Republicans hold only a one-vote majority — meaning losing one member would be…
articles.body:
The White House withdrew the nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) amid opposition from Senate Republicans, it confirmed to The Hill.

Overton was set to face a key vote Wednesday in the Senate health committee, where Republicans hold only a one-vote majority — meaning losing one member would be enough to sink the nomination if all Democrats oppose it.

GOP leaders could have attempted to take her nomination directly to the Senate floor without a committee vote, but such a move would have likely faced significant obstacles.

Overton serves as the deputy director of the White House’s Domestic Policy Council and has been closely involved in President Donald Trump’s health agenda.

Overton had an uphill battle since she was first tapped as the nominee to replace Marty Makary, who resigned in May. She faced questions from some Republicans as well as many prominent supporters of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr’s Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement.

Health committee chairman Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) has expressed concern over Overton’s role in Trump and Kennedy’s changes to vaccine policy. Last summer, Overton stood beside Trump when he announced an executive order to reduce and separate the childhood vaccine schedule. She called the action “historic,” spurring criticism from Cassidy.

During her confirmation hearing in September, Overton wouldn’t directly answer whether Trump was wrong and declined to say if she would stand up to the president or Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Overton was also questioned by Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) about abortion-related matters including the abortion pill mifepristone.

Overton is openly anti-abortion. She described the 2022 Supreme Court ruling overturning Roe v. Wade as “a huge victory for life.” During her hearing, she wouldn’t say directly whether she believes mifepristone is safe.

Former Kennedy senior adviser Calley Means, a prominent figure in the MAHA movement, said this month that Overton wrote a policy relaxing standards for fruit-flavored vapes.

He also alleged Overton helped the Justice Department “construct a legal argument” for why the Supreme Court should take up a case that involved shielding major chemical company Bayer from lawsuits connected to its pesticide products.

FDA has been roiled by an exodus of top staff and is viewed by many in the healthcare industry as less trustworthy and more politicized than it has been in any previous administration.

Some health industry analysts said the agency instability would likely continue under Overton. But it was not immediately clear who the administration is picking to replace her.

Senate HELP Committee chairman Bill Cassidy (R-La.) in a post on X took issue with the White House’s characterization that Overton did not have the votes.

Cassidy said he was having “productive conversations” with committee members and believed Overton would have cleared his committee. The final hangup, he said, was anti-abortion senators seeking assurances from the administration about its commitment to “life issues.”

“My conversations with her convinced me she would follow the science and push back against decisions that put Americans’ health at risk,” Cassidy wrote. “The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments. Unfortunately, with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats.”

articles.body:
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) threw his support behind proposed Medicare reforms from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is poised to serve as Speaker in the next Congress.

The independent senator told MS NOW’s Chris Hayes he was “very glad” to see the House Democratic leader’s proposal.

“If we can do it — and I think we can — this will substantially impact the lives of tens and tens of millions of people,” Sanders said.

The progressive lawmaker is positioned to chair the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions when Democrats take control in the next Congress.

On Wednesday, the lower chamber’s Democrats nominated Jeffries to be the next Speaker. Jeffries now awaits a final confirmation vote among the full body in January.

Democrats in both chambers have made health care reform a major issue headed into the 120th Congress. Shortly after the party’s sweeping victories in the midterm elections, in which they gained control of both chambers of Congress, Sanders reupped his call for passing “Medicare for All.”

While Jeffries’s plan stops short of instituting a universal single-payer healthcare system, it meets the immediate demands presented by Sanders and other progressives, including lowering the Medicare age from 65 to 55, expanding coverage to include dental, vision and hearing benefits and guaranteeing universal coverage for children.

“Right out of the gate, we will aggressively work on fixing the extraordinary damage that’s been done,” Jeffries said during a Tuesday press conference. “But we also know, as Democrats, that a return to the status quo is not acceptable.”

Texas Rep. Greg Casar (D), the chair of the House Progressive Caucus, supported these reforms in a social media post as a “Year 1 plan.”

“Step by step we will march toward healthcare as a human right and replace our broken, profit driven system,” he wrote.

The plan also drew support from Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.), who made passing Medicare for All a central pillar of his Senate campaign.

El-Sayed called these reform proposals “a great start” during an interview with MS NOW’s Jen Psaki on Tuesday.

“The challenge we sometimes have is we realize if we want to climb Mount Everest, none of us are Superman, so we can’t leap it in one tall bound,” he said.

“If that’s the base camp we need to get to, great, but understanding that it’s still not enough,” El-Sayed continued. “We will not have achieved the unmet promise in this country of healthcare that you can depend on from cradle to grave until we finally guarantee it to everybody.”

articles.title: Waymo suspends freeway rides, citing safety hazards
articles.summary: Waymo suspended freeway rides in its driverless vehicles across the U.S. following California’s temporary ban on the cars from highways. The autonomous taxi company told The Hill that after “recent freeway construction zone encounters” on a highway in the Golden State — which didn’t cause any injuries or collisions —the California Department of Motor Vehicles…
articles.body:
Waymo suspended freeway rides in its driverless vehicles across the U.S. following California’s temporary ban on the cars from highways.

The autonomous taxi company told The Hill that after “recent freeway construction zone encounters” on a highway in the Golden State — which didn’t cause any injuries or collisions —the California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) implemented restrictions.

“In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance,” Waymo wrote in a statement. “We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.”

The DMV explained that officials determined “Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety” because of “recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones,” according to a statement shared with The Hill.

One incident the DMV described showed a Waymo robotaxi attempting to pass two California Highway Patrol that were making a blockade on Interstate 280 in San Francisco. Another incident involved three of the company’s taxis entering an active construction zone near Burlingame, Calif.

Waymo first launched its driverless car service to consumers on California freeways in November 2025. In a blog post , the company touted its expansion onto freeways in Austin, Atlanta and parts of southern California.

In June, Waymo recalled nearly 4,000 robotaxis after it identified 13 instances of its vehicles driving into construction zones on highways in Arizona and California. This came after the company paused service on freeway operations in May, saying at the time, it was to improve how its vehicles navigated certain construction zones.

A California DMV official also told The Hill that before Waymo cars could resume service on freeways, the company had to provide “sufficient evidence that its vehicles can safely detect and respond to construction zones.”

The official warned that if the DMVs are not satisfied with the provided evidence, then the restrictions would remain in place.

articles.title: Iran attacks US air base in Kuwait
articles.summary: Iran on Wednesday targeted a U.S. air base in Kuwait and launched several attacks against Bahrain in a reemergence of tit-for-tat strikes in the Persian Gulf. The Iranian strikes, which came after American forces struck Tehran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, follow a quiet period between the two sides of roughly…
articles.body:
Iran on Wednesday targeted a U.S. air base in Kuwait and launched several attacks against Bahrain in a reemergence of tit-for-tat strikes in the Persian Gulf.

The Iranian strikes, which came after American forces struck Tehran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, follow a quiet period between the two sides of roughly two months.

A defense official told The Hill there was no impact to U.S. interests, referring further questions to Kuwait and Bahrain.

Bahrain and Kuwait said that they repelled the air attacks, with Iran’s military on Wednesday confirming its drones “targeted Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms belonging to the terrorist U.S. military at Ali Al-Salem Air Base in Kuwait,” according to Tehran’s state television.

The U.S. attack on Tuesday, meanwhile, involved a fighter aircraft using “precision munitions to strike an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) missile launch site on Qeshm Island in self-defense” in response to “IRGC aggression targeting U.S. personnel and assets,” according to the official.

Tehran also attempted to hit targets in Bahrain on Sunday and Friday. Washington has said all the attacks were intercepted.

Washington and Tehran since September have largely held off on retaliatory strikes as the two sides sought a diplomatic end to the war which began on Feb. 28.

But in the past week, as Iran struggles under the crushing economic weight of a U.S. blockade on its ports in the Strait of Hormuz since summer, it has stepped up attacks on U.S. targets and allies in the region.

On Friday, it targeted an American early warning radar facility in Bahrain as well as a radar system at a U.S. helicopter base there on Sunday. Tehran said the attacks were retaliation for reported U.S. strikes on its communications towers and drone surveillance.

U.S. Central Command, the military arm covering forces in the Middle East, said it remains “highly vigilant and fully postured to protect Americans across the region.”

President Trump, however , insists the conflict is “effectively over” even as he has not ruled out restarting major combat operations. On Tuesday, he also dismissed reports of a “ dirty bomb ” threat against D.C., saying the administration was keeping an eye on it.

articles.body:
Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) said Tuesday that he supports a Democratic proposal to expand healthcare access by lowering the eligibility age for Medicare and expanding access, a smaller step than some in the progressive wing are pushing for with Democrats’ new majority.

El-Sayed described the proposal as “a great start” to MS NOW’s Jen Psaki. “I think the challenge we sometimes have is we realize that if we want to climb Mount Everest, none of us are supermen, so we can’t leap it in one tall bound.”

Democrats campaigned on restoring cuts to Medicaid made by Trump’s signature tax bill and funding Affordable Care Act subsidies that Republicans did not renew .

But with the party set to reclaim some power in Washington, many Democrats, including House Speaker-elect Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.), now support going further than restoring cuts. Jeffries endorsed policies such as lowering the eligibility age for Medicare, expanding the services it covers and including children in the program.

El-Sayed supports Medicare For All, an ambitious progressive policy proposal that hopes to guarantee government-funded healthcare to all Americans, making it a central issue of his campaign. The senator-elect recently said he was willing to work with Trump on healthcare.

Jeffries and other Democratic leaders will have to contend with members of their caucus who are pushing the party to pass sweeping progressive reforms. Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), one of the House’s most left-wing members, announced her proposed legislative agenda Tuesday which included Medicare For All, abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and advancing reparations for Black Americans.

Still, even with a large majority in Congress, President Trump is unlikely to support most of Democrats’ policy priorities.

El-Sayed said that while he is pleased with the current suggestion of expanding healthcare without guaranteeing total access, he believes the party should not stop there.

“If that’s the base camp we need to get to, great, but understanding that it’s still not enough,” El-Sayed told Psaki. “We will not have achieved the unmet promise in this country of health care that you can depend on from cradle to grave until we finally guarantee it to everybody.”
